However, for Hong Kong China, their win over Uruguay tops everything else, as it came down to the final play. With no time left on the clock, the visitors squeezed out a penalty, and there was only one way forward: call for Paul Altier and ask their sharpshooter to send the ball through the posts.

With the kick set 40 metres from the Los Teros in-goal area, the winger put the ball on the tee and, without an ounce of doubt, punted the pill successfully over, sending him, his teammates, staff and supporters into raptures.

However, were his teammates as confident as Paul Altier in that moment? According to both Alexander Post and Matt Worley, yes.

“Paul’s confidence was the highest it has ever been, after that game against Chile in which he basically got every kick right. We had confidence he would put it over,” said Worley.

“French Paul doesn’t miss”, stated Alexandre Post. “And I was just wondering what celebration he was going to pull. The moment we got that pen, I was pretty sure he was going to slot it in.”

Hong Kong China were able to finish their July Nations Cup campaign in style after a slow start against Samoa, with former Northampton Saints and Bedford Blues player Matt Worley revealing how the team felt before that final match.

“I don’t think many people expected us to win at all, but we went in there with nothing to lose. Morale wasn’t where we wanted it to be before the game, but we went out there, played our game plan with a bit more freedom, and things started working. We capitalised on the momentum and ended up winning!”

After finally making their dream of qualifying for a Men’s Rugby World Cup come true, Hong Kong China’s senior national team has opened a new chapter in its high-performance programme, as the union reintroduced a full-time programme for more than 30 players.

Alexander Post, who played for Richmond over the past few seasons, was among those who returned to Hong Kong China under the new programme.

“The full-time programme was reintroduced, which I think has been pivotal for our latest development. Since we qualified for the Men’s Rugby World Cup, the programme was established, allowing players like Matt and me, who were playing abroad, to return to Hong Kong China and play full-time. It lets us focus on the details and push the team to take the next step up the ladder.”

Post, who was born and raised in Hong Kong, China, feels more positive about Hong Kong China’s future in the game as recent developments have finally borne fruit with the win against Uruguay, hopefully the first of many.

“You are always aiming to win every game that you are playing. Our head coach [Logan Asplin] says we don’t know where our ceiling is, and I agree, as some of our teammates weren’t full-time players before, and others were playing abroad,” stated the 30-year-old hooker.

“However, now that we’re working together week in, week out and putting in the hard work, we can go further in our goals and performances.”

Post and Worley have returned home after successful stints overseas, both featuring in the English Championship in recent years. Worley, who wore the Bedford Blues mantle for more than 100 games, holds special memories of a club that played a huge role in his career.

“I have great memories of the Champ and Bedford, as I stayed with them for six years and grew as a rugby player there. It’s a great league that’s been a bit neglected in the past, but not so much anymore, as I feel it’s got more attention. When I left, we were pretty close to full-time hours, completely different from when COVID hit.”

However, the utility back left out a vital piece of information about his impact in Bedford, prompting Post to step in and add it.

“There is a reason why they call Matt the king of Bedford!” reveals the experienced front-rower.

“The Champ is definitely neglected. It is a tough league packed with serious and great players. I learned a lot, and I can only thank Richmond for what they did for me. I loved every minute of it.”

While in England, the two faced each other several times, each enjoying their share of victories, and Post vividly recalls one particular encounter.

“We hosted the Blues and were down by 33 points at half-time, but we managed a 36-point comeback. I was on the bench and came on at half-time. Not saying I had anything to do with it, but it was nice to get one over Matt and Bedford! Facing London Scottish on New Year’s Day was also a pretty special memory.”

For Worley, however, that shared story is all but gone from his memory, though the Champ’s colour and character are still very much alive in his mind.

“I actually forgot about that game. I don’t recall it ever happening. Seriously, our trips to Cornish Pirates were always pretty great, as was the seven-hour bus trip, and we bonded as a team over it. Beating Ealing on their own ground is also another remarkable memory.”

title: How the All Blacks left ‘waarheid’ behind at the Garden of Eden
article_text:
There is the truth of the rugby world, and then there is the truth of South Africa. While the rest of the rugby world is dancing to the compulsive disco-beat under a glitterball of relentless attack, the world champions are waiting for the next World Cup and keeping their counsel; ready to pull the unwary back into the dark alleys outside and brawl with them in the gutter.

The 2026 Six Nations set a new record of 111 tries scored, and Les Bleus hardly noticed that they conceded the most tries [19] and points [130] of any winning campaign in the tournament’s history. The newly-minted Nations Championship in July promptly upped the ante, with an average of one extra converted try scored across the first three rounds.

Attacking records have been tumbling all around the rugby globe quicker than new heights set by pole-vaulter ‘Mondo’ Duplantis. Last weekend, the best two teams in the English Prem, Bath and Northampton, combined for a total of 18 tries and 119 points between them, with telly pundit Austin Healey comparing the game to one of the scoring extravaganzas in the NBA. Yes, the same Austin Healey who once memorably described the essence of the modern scrum as ‘16 guys who like food. They push. Sometimes they go up, sometimes they go down. The referee has a guess. Penalty. Lineout.’

The Greatest Rivalry series between New Zealand and the reigning double world champions temporarily dragged the dance choreography of all-out attack kicking and screaming back into the gutters. It was the most gripping event in the annual calendar thus far, a clash of two rugby worlds, and depictions of both beauty and beast alike were hung together along its storied walls.

It was like the Bayeux Tapestry of modern rugby, great forward warhorses flying into defensive shield-walls, the dead brutally stripped and dismembered at scrum and breakdown; finally, a green-and-gold arrow piercing the eye of the silver fern.

It will not be repeated. The temporary suspension of the Rugby Championship has illustrated a great divide in the game, and the two divergent forks in the road are growing too far apart, too quickly. South Africa has flirted with the dance floor via ‘Tony-ball’, but when pushover comes to shove, it believes in the gutters far more. Rassie Erasmus set the scene for the RGR series thus:

“You can see on social media, [the All Blacks] are advocating this high-intensity running, multi-phase, and ‘nobody can keep up with us’. [But] there are always three truths: New Zealand’s truth, the world’s truth, and then what we believe. There’s the waarheid – the Afrikaans word for truth.

“We think there’s a certain way to win World Cups, and we think that’s a grind. We think when you’re under pressure on your attack, it’s very tough to keep cohesion. If the pressure is very big, you start fumbling a few balls, and then you are stuck.

The first Bledisloe Cup game between Australia and New Zealand at the Garden of Eden Park provided further evidence that for better or worse, planet rugby is moving away from South Africa’s sphere of influence.

“When games are really, really ‘clutch-and-crunch’, you have a system that you can fall back on, which protects the players sometimes from not always having the confidence to do things.

“Since [Kiwi attack coach] Tony [Brown] has been with us, we feel we were attacking alright. We feel we’re doing not too badly, but we always want to keep the thing that we can fall back on when the pressure is really tough.”

Before the RGR series kicked off, the rest of the rugby world had aligned with New Zealand more than South Africa and it was flocking towards the bright lights, the dance-floor and avoiding the dark alleys of the game. When those traditional forward-biased heavyweights, France and England, have worked the new direction of the game out for themselves without any help from the shaky isles, you know you are well and truly on your own.

The first Bledisloe Cup game between Australia and New Zealand at the Garden of Eden Park provided further evidence that for better or worse, planet rugby is moving away from South Africa’s sphere of influence. Take a look at the following table, illustrating the progression of the All Blacks in some key areas from Nations Championship through RGR to the first Bledisloe Cup match:

As soon as New Zealand left South African shores, it is as if the pennies have dropped from the eyes and they are able to revert to ‘Nations Championship normal’. They comfortably hit their target of 100+ rucks set per game while losing less than one per cent to turnover, ball-in-play time rose effortlessly by over three minutes, and the total number of penalties dropped. Suddenly the scrum was no longer an issue and Irish referee Andrew Brace was able to navigate the entire game untroubled at set-piece.

What will All Blacks’ head coach Dave Rennie have learned from the 50-19 victory in Auckland, having been so mercifully released from the South African pressure-cooker? The four areas of weakness highlighted by the RGR series were the two set-pieces, the contestable aerial game, and discipline:

- Sub-par lineout. The lineout did not improve despite the continued selection of a natural lock [Tupou Vaa’i] at No.6. The set-piece is still fumbling its way forward at a sub-par average of 83% for the season.

title: What Jason Gilmore says Harlequins 'can’t tolerate' as winless run continues
article_text:
Harlequins head coach Jason Gilmore claimed his side restored pride despite a third successive loss of the Gallagher Prem campaign against Sale at CorpAcq Stadium in Salford.

The Sharks snatched a 28-24 win with a 73rd-minute penalty try after they had been outplayed for long periods by a Quins side smarting from last weekend’s 48-0 humiliation against Gloucester.

“It’s disappointing. We probably created three chances in the first half which we didn’t take which came back to bite us,” said Harlequins head coach Jason Gilmore.

“Fair play to Sale. They got themselves back into the game with their set-piece but I’m really proud of the boys’ efforts up here.

“Two bonus points on the road up here is, I wouldn’t say pleasing, but I’m just happy for the boys that they got some reward out of their work.

“If you’re prepared to go to dark places for us and win those collisions, then you’re going to get selected. If you’re dipping your toe in one week and then not the next, then we can’t tolerate that.

“You can’t be up one week and then down the next week like we had last week. Performance will dictate the shirts.”

Marcus Smith impressed with two tries on his return after injury and Harlequins hooker Sam Riley also touched down twice.

But Sale, who trailed 17-14 at the break, fought back with Ben Bamber adding to first-half tries from Elia Canakaivata and Gus Warr before the decisive late penalty try.

Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson admitted he was a relieved man after the late score awarded by referee Christophe Ridley after a maul, which had travelled 30 metres, had been pulled down illegally by the sin-binned Riley.

“We were looking down the barrel at 60 minutes. We were chasing the game all day,” said Sanderson. “We weren’t at the races but the fight’s in them clearly and it’s the second week they’ve found a way to win.

“They’ve had to manage the way through games…and come up with solutions and that’s really rewarding.

“I’m really, really proud of that but we’re still not where we want to be in terms of performance because that won’t be good enough against Glasgow next week. We know that but we’ll take the win.

“If you can win playing badly, then that’s a good sign. It’s up to us to step up but it’s all within our hands and our capabilities. That’s the exciting bit, isn’t it?”

title: Rachel Malcolm challenges Scotland to end losing streak after Australia collapse
article_text:
Scotland captain Rachel Malcolm wants her side to use the energy that will be generated around the quadruple header in Sydney on Saturday to their advantage and go out and put in a performance that they can be proud of.

The WXV Global Series clash between the Wallaroos and the Scots will kick things off at the Accor Stadium and will be followed by a men’s sevens match between Australia and Fiji, a women’s sevens match between Australia and New Zealand and then the Wallabies against the All Blacks in the second Bledisloe Cup Test of 2026.

So far this year Scotland have played in front of their own standalone record crowd of 30,498 at Scottish Gas Murrayfield when the Red Roses came calling during the Guinness Women’s Six Nations and then in front of 31,294 at the Aviva Stadium versus Ireland later in that same tournament.

But this coming weekend could be a different level in terms of everything that is going on at the Accor Stadium down under and back-row Malcolm wants her charges to embrace that and channel it into a good showing.

“What’s really cool about the women’s game nowadays is that we get the opportunity to play in these big showcase matches and we are all looking forward to the occasion, 100 percent,” the 35-year-old said.

“I think it is really exciting for us to be a part of the quadruple header and I think it’s brilliant that Australia have managed to get that sorted in terms of growing the game in general, growing the women’s game and getting more eyes on the women’s game.

“There’s two bits to it: one, we have to completely absorb and enjoy everything that is going to be going on around the fixture on the day and use it to energise ourselves for the game, but two, we cannot be overshadowed by that excitement.

“We’ve got to have our eye on what we’re up to in our game first and foremost and my job as captain is to keep the train on the tracks in that sense and keep us focused on performance.

“I’ve no doubt that we’ll be fine, whatever else is going on we want to go out there and perform.”

After losses to Canada, New Zealand and Australia last month in Edinburgh, Scotland’s WXV Global Series campaign concludes with Saturday’s match and then another meeting with the Wallaroos in Canberra on October 23.

While losses against number three in the world and two in the world Canada and New Zealand were expected, a defeat to Australia at Hive Stadium on Saturday 26 September was a real blow, especially after Scotland were 10-5 at half-time before losing 30-10.

It means that the Scots have now lost seven Tests in a row in all competition and are down to ninth in the world rankings with Australia sitting seventh.

And, ahead of the next game, the second half collapse against the Wallaroos last time out is still very much on the minds.

“I’ve been a part of this squad for a really long time and I’ve been a part of games like that that have ended up in a similar scoreline when things have got away from us,” Malcolm explained.

“But I’ve not been as frustrated at the end of a game before as I was than this one because I think the end result was probably fair.

“And I think it was fair based on how we performed in that second half.

“As players we didn’t do a good enough job in that second half and the real frustration is that we know we had it in us to go on and win the game.

“In the first half it felt like we were in control and we were in the driving seat, but that changed and since the game there have been a couple of really important learnings for what is a pretty inexperienced group around making the most of momentum when you have it.

“Taking opportunities when you have the wind is a big one. The conditions changed in the second half and they probably got a little bit worse in terms of the rain coming on as well and we left ourselves a mountain to climb.

“It’s definitely one that got away and I’m excited that we’ve now got two more opportunities to go and right those wrongs against the same opponents.

“I think it’s going to be a steeper challenge being away from home against the Wallaroos, but I have confidence going into these next two games that if we play as we know we can then we can give ourselves a real chance of getting wins.

“The belief is in this group, we just have to show that over 80 minutes and Sydney first up gives us a great chance to do that.

“We were prepped really well by our athletic performance team before we headed to Australia and we are ready for the next big game now.”

title: Rob Baxter: 'That was bloody stressful and I agree with her'
article_text:
Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter branded his side’s hard-fought victory over Newcastle which earned them a first Gallagher Prem victory of the season “bloody stressful”.

Exeter were careless and error-strewn as the lead changed hands on numerous occasions at Sandy Park before they got their noses in front for the final time to clinch a 34-28 success in front of a disappointing crowd of just over 7,000.

Newcastle overcame an awful start, going behind after only 40 seconds, to make life extremely difficult for the home side, Christian Wade scoring a hat-trick of tries.

Max Hicks added another, with Zack Henry converting all four to secure two valuable bonus points.

Ross Vintcent scored two tries for the Chiefs, while Sam Harris, Henry Slade and Bachuki Tchumbadze got the others, with Henry Slade converting three and kicking a penalty.

Baxter said: “My wife telephoned me after the game and said that was bloody stressful and I agree with her.

“We attacked well as we knew how to create opportunities, but we were badly lacking in defensive energy, being slow getting up off the floor.

“The flip-flopping of the lead prevented us from settling and the game didn’t have the control we would have liked.

“The pressure of the score line meant we didn’t take the simple options, but our defence did improve as they only scored once in the second half.”

Exeter also saw England wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso depart midway through the second half.

Baxter said: “He didn’t feel right as it seems he’s overloaded his hamstring a bit. It will be scanned, but at present it’s more of a concern than a worry.”

Despite the defeat, Newcastle director of rugby Dan McFarland was still upbeat.

He said: “To lose was disappointing, but two points against last season’s finalists was something to be proud of as every point gained in the Prem will have to be earned.

“We went down playing the brand of rugby that we want to play moving forward.

“We had opportunities to score early in the second half, but we made too many errors and there was a lack of connection.

“On 60 minutes, Jake Dalziel’s attempt for a 50/20 went the wrong way of the corner flag for us and that was a crucial moment.

“We have Scarlets away next week in a different competition and we will roll the dice as we’ve got a few players chomping at the bit to play.”

On Newcastle’s star performer Wade, McFarland added: “He’s a really good man, an excellent connector in our leadership group.

“He has dancing feet and exceptional speed and (is) a throwback as he’s not a modern day 6ft plus winger who has to keep competing in the air.”

title: Double Bok World Cup winner’s future hangs in balance as ruling looms
article_text:
South Africa hooker Bongi Mbonambi is reportedly awaiting the outcome of a lengthy disciplinary hearing at the Sharks over alleged misconduct during a pre-season team-building camp in August.

According to South African outlet Rapport, the 35-year-old was involved in an incident at Bayala Private Safari Lodges before the Sharks’ August 11 fixture against the All Blacks. Head coach JP Pietersen had reportedly allowed players to socialise on a Tuesday evening before returning to full training, but Mbonambi, Trevor Nyakane and Eduan Swart allegedly continued into Wednesday morning.

Fez Mbatha is also said to have missed a team activity the following morning after a late night. Mbatha and Swart have subsequently received written warnings, with their cases reportedly treated as first offences. Nyakane is understood to be in a different position because he was not present when Pietersen set out the team rules.

Mbonambi’s case has taken longer to resolve, with a ruling from the presiding officer expected within the next two weeks. Reports in South Africa have suggested the outcome could have significant implications for his future at the Durban franchise. The 82-cap Bok’s contract is not due to expire until 2028, but it could potentially be terminated early.

The double World Cup winner has not featured for the Sharks in the opening rounds of the URC and is not currently training with the squad, despite reports that he is fit enough to play.

Asked about Mbonambi’s absence last week, Pietersen said: “Bongi is obviously not available. There is no comment on Bongi.”

The situation also leaves uncertainty over the veteran hooker’s international prospects. Mbonambi has not played for the Springboks since facing Wales in Cardiff last November and has since dealt with knee and back injuries which, combined with his current situation, have kept him out of action since January.

South Africa are due to face Italy, Ireland and France in November, meaning the timing of the ruling could have consequences for his hopes of returning to the Test set-up before the end of the year. Worse still, it could seriously hamper, or even end, any hopes he has of forcing his way back into Rassie Erasmus’ Springbok plans and making a tilt at a third World Cup title next year.

title: ‘I'm inspired’: Why an All Blacks veteran still draws inspiration from his younger brother
article_text:
Running out alongside your two brothers for the All Blacks would be special enough once, let alone 54 times, but veteran playmaker Beauden Barrett continues to draw inspiration from his younger brothers.

Barrett started his first Test match of the 2026 season against the Wallabies at Eden Park, lacing up the boots alongside two of his younger brothers, Scott and Jordie, for the 54th time at Test level.

Scott, who has now played 90 Tests, returned from a serious back injury after a non-playing sabbatical for the Crusaders, while Jordie continued where he left off after recent standout performances in Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series against South Africa.

Speaking to New Zealand-based media from the All Blacks’ hotel in Sydney, the 146-Test first-five admitted it was a special night at Eden Park for multiple reasons.

“At home, every time it’s a privilege. But yeah, having missed out on recent Test matches, it means a lot to get back out there and to play alongside my brothers,” the experienced playmaker said.

“Especially, you know, with Scott’s return, and that always feels really good. But this one was super special.”

Jordie claimed man-of-the-match honours for the All Blacks, accumulating a mammoth 16 tackles and thirteen carries, ferociously hitting anything and everything wearing green and gold at Eden Park.

The midfielder’s older brother, Beauden, was in awe of his performance, saying he’s “hands down” the best No.12 in the world at this current moment in time.

“Oh, he’s been incredible this season. Every single Test match I’m inspired by his work rate, his physicality, and his involvement; his influence on this team is second to none.

“So yeah, I’m just proud as a big brother and the way that he’s leading. I guess you don’t get to see that from outside the environment, but he’s certainly matured into a world-class player.

Despite only featuring for a staggering nine minutes in Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry Test matches, Barrett looked assured in his fullback role and his ability to influence the game in multiple facets.

Barrett explained on Monday that he had clear intentions going into Saturday night’s first Bledisloe Cup Test in Auckland.

“Yeah, [I] felt great. I just wanted to go out there and work hard, communicate really well, and have fun.

“So, yeah, obviously we had to work for it. It was a proper test match in terms of the scoreboard; it was very tight for 50 minutes, and we had to really roll our sleeves up and embrace those moments.

“That’s what test matches are all about. And we’ve learned a lot from that one as well. We know that it’s just a start. We’ve seen areas that we want to really hone in on and be better at.

“We’re certainly not satisfied, and we’ve got a lot of work to do.”

A hat-trick from Newcastle wing Christian Wade was not enough to stop Exeter claiming their first Gallagher Prem win of the season as they edged a topsy-turvy game at Sandy Park 34-28.

The lead frequently changed hands and it was not until the dying stages that the Chiefs were able to seal victory.

Max Hicks scored Newcastle’s other try, with Zack Henry converting all four to secure two valuable bonus points.

Ross Vintcent scored two tries for an error-ridden Exeter, while Sam Harris, Henry Slade and Bachuki Tchumbadze got the others, with Slade converting three and kicking a penalty.

It took Exeter just 40 seconds to open the scoring when Vintcent charged down a clearance kick to gather and score.

Three minutes later Newcastle were level when a long pass from an alert Simon Benitez Cruz gave Wade an easy run-in.

The frenetic opening continued as a well-timed pass from Slade sent Vintcent galloping 20 metres down the right flank to score his second try before skilful handling from the visitors allowed Hicks to cross, with Henry’s conversion putting them in front for the first time.

A fifth try arrived before the first quarter had elapsed, with Slade racing through a leaky defence for an individual score, but Exeter then suffered a blow when flanker Ethan Roots was yellow-carded for a no-arms tackle.

Newcastle also suffered a setback when their full-back Harrison Obatoyinbo departed for an HIA, to be replaced by Jake Dalziel, who became the club’s youngest ever league debutant aged just 18 years and 54 days.

Dalziel almost made a dream start when his well-judged cross-field kick picked out Werner Kok in acres of space, but a horrible bounce for the wing prevented a certain score.

However, Red Bulls were able to take advantage of Roots’ absence when a break from Sammy Arnold provided Wade with his second.

Roots returned from the sin-bin, but Newcastle still led 21-19 at the end of a pulsating first half.

Four minutes after the restart the home side were back in front when a period of pressure was rewarded with the bonus-point try from Harris, on his Prem debut.

However, a handling error from Slade presented Wade with the opportunity to complete his hat-trick, a kick-and-chase securing the touchdown.

Exeter suffered a further blow when Immanuel Feyi-Waboso departed with a leg problem before Red Bulls introduced hooker Samson Adejimi for his debut.

The hosts also made changes by bringing on back-rowers Tom Hooper and Kane James in an attempt to reverse their fortunes and it paid dividends when a Slade penalty gave them a one-point lead before Tchumbadze crashed over to wrap up victory, with Newcastle prop Adam Brocklebank sin-binned.

title: Sale complete late win to leave Harlequins bottom of table

Harlequins’ troubled start to the Gallagher Prem season continued with a third successive loss of the campaign against Sale at CorpAcq Stadium in Salford.

The Sharks left it late but came from behind to snatch a 28-24 success with a 73rd-minute penalty try, after the returning Marcus Smith had touched down twice in the opening quarter to threaten a shock win for the visitors.

After their opening-day reverse to Bristol at home, Sale have bounced back strongly with back-to-back wins over Saracens and Quins.

But despite their first points of the season, the loss leaves Jason Gilmore’s team – who suffered their worst league defeat in 26 years last weekend, a 48-0 humbling by Gloucester – rooted to the foot of the table.

With Smith involved for the first time this season after a finger injury, the visitors made seven changes on the back of that embarrassment.

This was a big improvement on that toothless display but, with a late power surge, Sale found a way to chalk up what was their fifth successive win against Harlequins in the league and Europe.

Quins, who had two tries disallowed before the interval, deserved their 17-14 half time lead.

They made a fast start with hooker Sam Riley giving them a third-minute lead, diving over in the corner after Smith and George Furbank had combined in midfield.

Five minutes later Smith was over after a beautiful tip pass from Furbank had freed Luke Northmore down the right wing.

Sale hit back in the 11th minute with a superb try of their own from Fijian number eight Elia Canakaivata on his first Prem start, with Jacques Vermeulen suspended after his red card against Saracens.

Smith went through some weak defence for his second try in the 19th minute and only a brilliant cover tackle from O’Flaherty prevented the England man grabbing his hat-trick inside the first half hour.

Sale cut the deficit two minutes before the break with scrum-half Gus Warr going over after some nice work in midfield from Alex Lozowski.

With the Sharks conceding too many penalties, Riley was mauled over for Quins’ bonus-point try in the 53rd minute.

But when Sale finally were able to hold onto possession, second row Ben Bamber crossed after an initial break by Nicky Smith.

Quins pressed again but a crucial lineout steal from Courtney Lawes dug the Sharks out of a hole. Then Chandler Cunningham-South was unable to find Cadan Murley after intercepting George Ford’s pass.

But then Sale’s pack got rumbling with seven minutes left, mauling Quins back 30 metres before Riley pulled it down close to the tryline and conceded a penalty try. The hooker was sent to the sin-bin and the visitors, chasing the game short-handed, could not find a way back.

title: Zverev secures year-end number one ranking
article_text:
Alexander Zverev is guaranteed to finish the 2026 season as world number one after Carlos Alcaraz's surprise defeat in the Shanghai Masters.

German Zverev was on course to climb above current world number one Jannik Sinner, who has been ruled out for the rest of the year with a knee injury.

Alcaraz still had a mathematical chance of stopping Zverev until he was beaten 7-5 7-6 (7-4) by Belgium's Zizou Bergs in the third round on Monday.

"It's been a fantastic season for me. Knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true," said Zverev.

After losing three major finals, Zverev landed the first Grand Slam title of his career by winning the French Open in June, and followed that with victory at the US Open last month.

The 29-year-old has taken advantage of the injury problems suffered by Spaniard Alcaraz and Italian Sinner - the dominant pair on the ATP Tour in the previous two seasons - to become the world's leading player.

Zverev cannot overtake Sinner until 2 November at the earliest.

He will become the first German man to end the year as number one, and the oldest player to achieve the feat for the first time.

After suffering a serious ankle injury in the 2022 French Open semi-finals which kept him out for seven months, Zverev regained his place in the upper echelons of the sport and been ranked inside the top four continuously since March 2024.

"So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style," he added.

At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Alcaraz would finish it as world number one.

Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500.

The dominance of the pair - who split all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field.

Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the rankings than the top two.

But as the season enters its final stretch, Zverev has completed what many thought was impossible.

There is no escaping the fact that Zverev has benefitted from Sinner and Alcaraz missing large chunks of the season through injury, meaning he won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent.

Both his major wins came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until beating Ben Shelton in the New York final.

Zverev has said he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game".

But, as the old adage goes, you can only beat what is in front of you.

Zverev has done exactly that to record the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since he emerged as a teenage prodigy.

Alcaraz has made encouraging progress since returning from a wrist injury which kept him off tour for almost five months, but this was a reminder that coming back from such a long absence is not smooth sailing.

The seven-time Grand Slam champion was below the level he showed in winning the Japan Open last week as he produced a string of uncharacteristic errors.

"Today wasn't a good match from my side. I didn't feel good," said Alcaraz, who also credited 39th-ranked Bergs for serving strongly and taking his chances.

"Right now, all the negative thoughts come to my mind and none of the positives, but I think [later] I will take the good things."

Bergs, who showed great composure to serve out the biggest win of his career, faces American Tommy Paul in the last 16.

Zverev remains in the draw as one of only three top-eight seeds left, alongside Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime and Russia's Daniil Medvedev.

title: Fit-again Kartal beats top-50 opponent in Wuhan
article_text:
Sonay Kartal says she has "thrown herself in the deep end" since returning from a six-month injury absence after beating Anhelina Kalinina to reach the Wuhan Open second round.

The British number five, 24, reached the third round at the Beijing Open earlier this month in her first WTA tournament since suffering a stress fracture in her back.

She followed that up by defeating Ukraine's Kalinina 7-5 6-3 in an hour and 31 minutes in Wuhan.

World number 170 Kartal will face Swiss ninth seed Belinda Bencic next.

"I've thrown myself in the deep end, playing [my] first few events playing the best players in the world," said Kartal.

"It's definitely a challenge, but I'm happy with the level that I've managed to produce. There is still got a long way to go to get to back where I left off, but I'm happy. It's looking positive and I'm feeling good."

Kartal returned to action last month for Great Britain at the Billie Jean King Cup team event, where she narrowly lost to Czech Marie Bouzkova, who sat 26th in the world rankings.

Wins over Spain's Andrea Lazaro Garcia and Wang Xinyu followed for Kartal in Beijing, before she lost to Armenia's Alina Charaeva.

Against world number 48 Kalinina, Kartal served four aces and won 23 of 30 points when landing her first serve.

She sealed her spot in the last-32 stage at the third time of asking after Kalanina saved two match points.

Zheng Qinwen withdrew from her home tournament in Wuhan after becoming the first Chinese player to win the China Open.

In a statement, Zheng said she would not be competing because her "body is feeling very fatigued" after "an intense run of matches".

Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and had struggled with form and fitness over the past 12 months, before a recent upturn led to her triumph in Beijing.

title: Karaoke-singing Zheng makes history with China Open win
article_text:
Zheng Qinwen became the first Chinese woman to win the China Open by beating Mirra Andreeva in Beijing.

Zheng, who entered the tournament as a wildcard ranked number 54 in the world, saved three set points in Sunday's opener before overcoming fourth seed Andreeva 7-5 6-4.

The 24-year-old fell to the floor after converting match point and treated the raucous home crowd to some karaoke following her victory speech.

"The feeling was incredible. To win here in Beijing in front of my home crowd is one of my dreams," she said.

"I've been through a very, very tough year."

For Zheng, who underwent elbow surgery last year, it was a first WTA 1000 title and her sixth title over all. The triumph brings an end to a two-year title drought for a player who has struggled with form and fitness in the past 12 months.

Andreeva, 19, was on top in the early stages of both sets, but was reeled back in both times.

The Russian led 2-0 in both sets and 5-4 in the first before Zheng saved three set points and won the remaining 11 points to win the opener 7-5.

Andreeva continued to make mistakes in a second set that was finely poised at 4-4 before Zheng took control.

The crowd was passionate, although disruptive at times between points, and a late double fault from Zheng in the final exchanges briefly threatened to derail a special occasion for Chinese tennis.

But there was to be no late collapse and Zheng sealed the win with an ace.

"I felt like I just forgot how to compete after coming back from injury," she told reporters.

"Finally, after so many losses, I [found] my fire again," she said.

The win is her 14th win over a top-10 opponent and her third this season.

Despite the loss, Andreeva is expected to rise to number three in the world when the rankings are updated on Monday.

Zheng is set to leap up 31 spots to number 23 and will compete at Wuhan Open on Tuesday.

"I'm so hungry, honestly, for what's going to come next," Zheng said.

title: Highlights as Carlos Alcaraz was dumped out in the third round of the Shanghai Masters by Zizou Bergs
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz was dumped out in the third round of the Shanghai Masters as Zizou Bergs recorded the biggest win of his career, with the Spaniard's defeat confirming Alexander Zverev as the year-end world No 1.

Bergs beat the second seed 7-5 7-6 (7-4), recovering to win the second set in a tie-break after failing to serve out the match at 6-5.

Alcaraz's exit, coupled with current world No 1 Jannik Sinner ending his campaign early due to a knee problem that has sidelined him since Wimbledon, means Zverev will end 2026 top of the rankings for the first time.

Zverev, who won the French Open and US Open this summer for his maiden major titles, said of his achievement: "It's been a fantastic season for me winning in Paris and New York and knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true.

"So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style."

Alcaraz, who won the Japan Open in Tokyo last Tuesday, was chasing a ninth ATP Masters 1000 title and his first of an injury-hit season.

However, it is Bergs who will now face USA's Tommy Paul in the next round after he beat defending champion Valentin Vacherot 6-4 6-2.

Bergs converted three of the four break points he manufactured - Alcaraz went two from two on that metric - and notched 24 winners compared to the Spaniard's 16.

The world No 39 said: "It is a bit of disbelief and not feeling too much. It is one of the moments you don't really realise what it going on, you are just in the moment, focused on the points you have to play

"I am very happy how I handled the tie-break. It is never easy when you get broken serving for the match but in the tie-break I played the key moments and served big.

"I often have too much respect for these guys. That is part of the culture and I am proud of that but it is a little bit in the way when you play them.

"I had a moment here last year against Novak Djokovic where I was definitely playing the name not the guy, so to have this moment [against Alcaraz] is a relief.

"I now feel I can win against those guys, not just play against them."

Elsewhere, 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev - defaulted at last week's China Open in Beijing after hitting a fan with a ball while facing Djokovic in the semi-finals - joined Bergs in round four after a straight-sets victory over qualifier Dalibor Svrcina.

Medvedev will take on Stefanos Tsitsipas next after the Greek upset 11th seed Taylor Fritz 3-6 7-5 6-3.

At the Wuhan Open in China, Britain's Sonay Kartal defeated top-50 opponent Anhelina Kalinina to set up a second-round clash with ninth seed Belinda Bencic.

Kartal recently returned from a six-month absence with a stress fracture in her back, reaching the third round of the Beijing Open last week in her first WTA tournament back.

The British No 5 - whose compatriot Katie Boulter begins her campaign against 11th seed Diana Schnaider on Tuesday - won 7-5 6-2 win in 91 minutes, hitting four aces.

Kartal said: "I've thrown myself in the deep end, playing [my] first few events playing the best players in the world. It's definitely a challenge, but I'm happy with the level that I've managed to produce.

"There is still got a long way to go to get to back where I left off, but I'm happy. It's looking positive and I'm feeling good."

In the most eye-catching match of the day, Xiyu Wang thrashed namesake Xinyu Wang 6-2 6-0, with Xiyu's reward a second-round tie against Slovakia's Mia Pohankova.

This result was an upset with Xiyu ranked 91st in the world and Xinyu at 39.

title: China Open: Qinwen Zheng stuns Mirra Andreeva to make history as first Chinese winner of WTA event in Beijing
article_text:
Olympic champion Qinwen Zheng made history as the first Chinese player to win the China Open on Sunday, stunning French Open winner Mirra Andreeva 7-5 6-4.

Wild card Zheng, who has been on a recovery path after missing nearly six months due to an elbow injury on her dominant right arm, looked like her old self as she used powerful forehands to control the rallies, and landed swift winners angling away from Andreeva.

After the two exchanged early breaks, world No 5 Andreeva held firm to go 5-4 up, and almost got a decisive break when Zheng sent a cross-court shot too long before netting a forehand.

However, Zheng saved three break points to make it 5-5, and pounced on an error-prone Andreeva in the next game, outwitting the Russian with a swift backhand to get the break that secured the first set.

Andreeva saved three break points as the second set was poised at 4-4, but a persistent Zheng got the break, and landed a perfect ace in the next game to clinch her first WTA 1000 title on home soil.

Zheng and Andreeva have since withdrawn from this week's Wuhan Open, with Zheng citing a right shoulder issue and tiredness as her reasons and Andreeva's absence due to a change of schedule.

Zheng said in a statement released by the WTA: "Since returning from injury... I have played a demanding stretch of tennis over the past month and a half, competing at the US Open, the Billie Jean King Cup and the China Open.

"My body is feeling very fatigued after this intense run of matches. I look forward to returning to the Wuhan Open next year and stepping onto the court in my best possible form!"

Top-seeded Alexander Zverev let two match points slip in the second-set tiebreaker before winning 6-4 6-7 (6-8) 6-3 against Quentin Halys at the ATP 1000 Shanghai Masters on Sunday.

Zverev never gave up a break-point chance in a third-round match where the US Open champion needed seven of his own just to break the 48th-ranked Frenchman's service in the opening game.

Earlier on Sunday, US Open finalist Ben Shelton was beaten 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (7-33) by 21-year-old Frenchman Arthur Gea in the third round. The third-seeded Shelton, who won his first match in Shanghai on his 24th birthday, saw Gea convert his first match-point chance in the second-set tiebreaker.

Ninth-seeded Alex de Minaur beat Rei Sakamoto 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 and 26th-seeded Karen Khachanov defeated Adrian Mannarino 6-2 6-4.

No 1-ranked Jannik Sinner withdrew from Shanghai this week when he announced he was taking the rest of 2026 off because of a right knee injury.

Zverev is closing in on finishing the season as world No 1 for the first time and found himself playing an extra set Sunday.

Twice Halys faced match point while serving in the tiebreaker, saved both, then clinched the set with an overhead volley winner at the net. Zverev regained control of the match by breaking Halys's first service game of the deciding set.

In the round of 16, Zverev will play Alexander Bublik who rallied to beat Brandon Nakashima 6-7 (7-9) 6-3 7-6 (7-5).

title: What Carlos Alcaraz was heard yelling at his coach during Shanghai Masters loss to Zizou Bergs
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz struggled in his third-round match against Zizou Bergs in the third round of the Shanghai Masters.

The Spaniard arrived at the penultimate Masters tournament of the calendar in good form, having lifted the Japan Open title for the second year in a row.

He began his campaign with a solid straight-sets victory against Juan Manuel Cerundolo in his opening round match in Shanghai, but he did not play his best tennis as he lost in straight sets to Bergs.

Alcaraz was broken twice in the first set against Bergs, in a set that he would go on to lose 7-5 to continue his worrying displays in the opening sets on the ATP Tour’s Asian swing.

He followed it up by losing a second set tie-break to confirm his exit from the Shanghai Masters.

The Spaniard appeared to be struggling with the conditions in Shanghai and he was letting his coach, Samuel Lopez, know about it during the match.

“I can’t play like this. A ball that goes like this and bounces like this… I don’t understand it,” said Alcaraz during the first set. “You can’t play tennis by instinct.”

Alcaraz’s early defeat continues a bizarre run for the Spaniard at the Shanghai Masters.

The star has played the Chinese Masters tournament on three occasions and he has never reached past the quarterfinals of the event.

The star was knocked out of the fourth round in 2023, to Grigor Dimitrov, while he reached the last eight in his best effort a year later, where he lost to Tomas Machac.

Alcaraz opted not to play the tournament in 2025, but his return in 2026 continues his disappointing trajectory at the Masters 1000 event.

His early exit in 2026 means he has a 6-3 win-loss record at the tournament, which equates to a winning percentage of 66.6% at the Shanghai Masters.

That means the Shanghai Masters is Alcaraz’s third worst performing Masters 1000 event, which is a major worry for the current world No 3.

Only the Paris Masters and the Canadian Open are worse, with Alcaraz currently sitting at a 50% win rate at both of those tournaments.

Unsurprisingly, Alcaraz is yet any of those three tournaments, as they continue to elude him in his quest to collect all of the Masters events on the ATP Tour calendar.

Alcaraz will next be in action at the Six Kings Slam, which between October 21st and 24th, and will air internationally on Netflix.

title: Alex Eala ranking points and prize money after Wuhan Open setback
article_text:
Alex Eala’s recent struggles continued after she was dumped out of the Wuhan Open by world No 201 Han Shi in the first round.

The 21-year-old has found wins hard to come by since her third-round loss to Iva Jovic at the US Open in September. The left-hander lost her opener at the Singapore Open to Tatiana Prozorova, who at the time was ranked 180th in the world.

Despite being the heavy favourite for the gold medal at the Asian Games, Eala then lost in the semi-finals to Wang Xiyu, and now, she has lost again, this time in Wuhan on Monday.

Eala took the first set 6-4 but then the Chinese qualifier bounced back to take the second 3-6. The youngster lost seven games in a row and was powerless to stop Shi taking the decider 6-3.

As a result of this setback at the WTA 1000 event, the world No 19 picks up just 10 points and $18,300 (£13,854) in prize money. She is on 2,241 points in the live WTA rankings and is 18th in the Race on 2,151 ranking points.

Even though her form has taken a turn for the worse, Eala still has a shot at finishing the year in the top 20. Madison Keys is 19th in the Race, with 2,094 points, but isn’t playing in Wuhan, nor is China Open champion Zheng Qinwen (2,018 points).

It would appear that Eala is running out of energy as the season winds down. This year, her win-loss record is 40/23, in what has been a demanding season.

It seems Eala has not been able to hit the heights she achieved at the Washington Open when she beat Elina Svitolina, Naomi Osaka, and Jessica Pegula on her way to her first WTA Tour title.

After this early Wuhan exit, Eala still has a chance to end the Asian Swing on a more positive note, though.

Next Monday, the WTA 500 tournament in Ningbo, China, gets underway, and then on 26 October, the Toray Pan Pacific Open Tennis event (also a 500) in Tokyo begins.

Eala is out of the running to play in the WTA Finals in Indian Wells in November but she still has time to end her season on a high.

title: Carlos Alcaraz vs Zizou Bergs controversy sparks calls for major tennis rule change after ‘unacceptable’ incident
article_text:
Zizou Bergs secured an unforgettable victory over Carlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Open but the Belgian has been criticised for his actions during the third-round match.

Bergs upset second seed Alcaraz in just over two hours in a 7-5, 7-6 (4) victory at Qizhong Forest Sports City Arena on Monday for the biggest win of his career.

The 27-year-old was, naturally, emotional after this major scalp, particularly as he has struggled to get over the line in big matches.

He said afterwards, “This is something that has been very tough for me. I often have too much respect for these guys, which is part of my culture and I’m proud of that. But it gets a little bit in the way when you have to play them. I had a great moment here last year against [Novak] Djokovic where I was definitely playing the name, not the guy.

“The more experience you have practising against them and playing matches, the more it becomes the new standard a little bit. To have this moment, for me it is a little bit of a relief. I feel like now I really can win against these guys. Not just I can play against them, but I can win against them.”

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

However, his conduct during the contest has been called into question by former British star Jamie Murray, who criticised Bergs for taking a near 10-minute bathroom break after winning the first set.

In regards to toilet breaks, journalist Jose Moron pointed out that the ATP rulebook states, “The time will start counting from the moment the tennis player enters the bathroom, and they can take a maximum of three minutes, with two extra minutes if there is a change of clothes.”

However, he claimed that Bergs took nine and a half minutes and didn’t receive a warning from the chair umpire.

He questioned why is there is rule if umpires don’t enforce it and two-time men’s doubles slam winner Murray, who is Andy Murray’s older brother, said something similar.

He tweeted, “Over eight minutes for a toilet break. Still not started back. Probably takes 20 seconds to walk from centre court to the changing rooms in Shanghai. How is that acceptable/allowed?”

Over 8mins for a toilet break. Still not started back. Prob takes 20 secs to walk from centre court to the changing rooms in Shanghai. How is that acceptable/allowed?

Andre Agassi’s former coach, Brad Gilbert, said this happens far too much, there needs to be clearer rules put in place, and if players fall afoul of them, punishments should be handed out.

The American tweeted in response to Murray, “Unfortunately, happens all too often. There needs to be way clearer rules on comfort breaks.

“Should only be allowed, in my humble opinion, on set breaks; three minutes or five minutes with gear change, then if not ready, lose a point [for] every 30 seconds.”

title: Alexander Zverev’s first words as US Open champion clinches year-end No 1 after Carlos Alcaraz loss
article_text:
Alexander Zverev says it is a “dream come true” that he will finish 2026 as the year-end No 1.

With Jannik Sinner out for the rest of the season with a knee injury, Zverev was destined to finish the year as the world’s top-ranked player.

However, Carlos Alcaraz’s surprise third-round loss to Zizou Bergs at the Shanghai Open means nobody can catch the 29-year-old in the ATP Tour rankings.

The German has enjoyed a magical year, winning both the French Open and US Open to finally break his Grand Slam duck. Now, the 6ft 6in player has opened up on a “fantastic” season that is getting better and better.

He told the ATP’s website, “It’s been a fantastic season for me, winning in Paris and New York and knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

“So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style.”

Zverev has been leading the ATP Race to Sinner by 900 points, with the world No 2 currently sitting on 8,850 points. Australian Open champion Alcaraz is back in third on 4,600 points, with US Open finalist Ben Shelton fourth on 4,480.

But with the Spaniard’s Shanghai Open exit, Zverev now has an unassailable lead in the Race and cannot be caught until 2027 at the earliest.

The ATP states he will be 29 years and 217 days old on the date of the year-end ATP Rankings (23 November). Plus, he will be three years older than Andre Agassi was in 1999 and 20 days older than Andy Murray was in 2016.

On social media, Zverev posted a number of graphics that said ‘2026 year-end world No 1’, including a Bitpanda montage of this new milestone.

ATP Chairman Andrea Gaudenzi added, “Finishing the season as year-end No. 1 is the ultimate achievement in our sport. Congratulations to Sascha, who became just the 20th player to do so.

“For a decade, he has consistently been one of the best players in the world. To finish as year-end No. 1 for the first time aged 29 shows his grit and determination to continue pushing forward.”

For now, he will focus on trying to win the Shanghai Masters, where he is into the last 16 to face Alexander Bublik.

title: Carlos Alcaraz opens up on ‘negative thoughts’ after surprise Shanghai Masters defeat
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz says it is “really difficult” to take any positives from his straight-set loss to Zizou Bergs at the Shanghai Masters.

After winning his first title since returning from a wrist injury at the Japan Open last week, Alcaraz was much more sluggish against an inspired Bergs on Monday.

The Belgian was not overawed by the occasion and closed out a 7-5, 7-6 (4) third-round victory. The 27-year-old served for the match at 6-5 but was broken back immediately to set up a tiebreak.

However, Bergs did not need a second invitation as he claimed the biggest win of his career in just over two hours inside Qizhong Forest Sports City Arena.

After winning the ATP 500 event in Tokyo less than a week ago, in what was his first title for half a year after being out for more than four months with a wrist issue, this was a reality check for the Spaniard.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Although Alcaraz is feeling optimistic about his chances over the coming weeks, he did lift the lid on his immediate “negative thoughts”.

When asked if he is still feeling positive about the rest of the season, Alcaraz told reporters, “Yeah, of course. I mean, I played great tournaments. Obviously, taking the positive things from today is really difficult. Right now, I didn’t take it yet.

“So, I will try the next few days to think clearly. Right now, you know, all the negative thoughts come to my mind and none of the positives. But I think I will take it, you know, the good things about, you know, having the matches.

“I can re-watch the matches with my coach, with my team. It’s going to be really helpful for the next tournament. But just happy with the way that I’m playing lately, and obviously positive tournaments, the latest ones.”

Bergs won eight points more than Alcaraz in the match; the former world No 1 hit 16 winners to 27 unforced errors, and he won just 21 per cent of first serve return points, as the Belgian’s delivery kept him at arm’s length.

And Alcaraz’s lack of accuracy and consistency was a big bugbear for him.

Asked if he was less satisfied with his tennis than usual, he replied, “Well, I would say everything. To be honest, I didn’t play the way that I wanted to play, a lot of mistakes. I didn’t find a good position on the return. For example, I was returning pretty well. Today I didn’t find a good one. Obviously, credit to him. I would say he serves really, really well.

“But when I got into the rhythm, when I got into the point, I made a lot of mistakes. I wasn’t feeling comfortable with the shots. So, I’m really disappointed with today’s match, because I didn’t find the solution. I would say I just made a lot of unforced errors.”

Alcaraz only returned from his wrist problem at the US Open, where he made the quarter-finals. Encouraging displays at the Laver Cup were backed up by his title success in Tokyo.

He has only played a handful of tournaments since his injury comeback, so this isn’t a huge setback for world No 3 Alcaraz.

title: How Carlos Alcaraz’s Shanghai Masters exit affects ATP Rankings as world No 3 suffers blow
article_text:

title: Zizou Berg’s immediate reaction after stunning win over Carlos Alcaraz in Shanghai
article_text:
Zizou Bergs was not quite sure “what was going on” after his stunning win over Carlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Masters, admitting he was in “disbelief”.

The world No 39 claimed the biggest win of his career as he beat seven-time Grand Slam winner Alcaraz 7-5, 7-6 (7-5) in just over two hours in the third round of the ATP Masters 1000 event.

It is only his third top-10 win following victories over world No 9 Andrey Rublev at the 2025 Miami Open and world No 5 Felix Auger-Aliassime at this year’s United Cup.

Alcaraz was the overwhelming favourite as he is fresh from winning the Japan Open and also cruised past Juan Manuel Cerundolo in the second round, but never got his nose in front as the Belgian broke in game five before the second seed got back on terms in the next game.

Bergs, though, claimed the crucial break in 11, but the second set had a similar theme with the Belgian breaking first only for Alcaraz to hit back. This time Bergs went on to get the job done in the tie-breaker.

Naturally, the 27-year-old was stunned after his win saying: “It’s a little about disbelief and not feeling too much. These are some of the moments where you don’t realise what’s going on.

“You’re just really in the moment, focused on the points you have to play. It’s tough to calm down a little bit, but I’ll be very happy.

“I obviously just tried to play my game. I felt like last week in Tokyo I really was in good shape. This week in training as well, I’m feeling the ball, being aggressive, and also serving quite well.

“My percentage is really high in the last number of matches, we’ve really worked on it, and it gives me a little bit of breathing room. I have a very good return and if I serve well we can utilise that even more.”

Bergs claimed a late mini break in the tie-breaker and then served it out.

He added: “I’m very happy how I handled the tie-break. He’s never easy to get broken when you can serve for the match. Really, to get back into the tie-break, play those key moments, serve big, I’m very happy with that one especially.

“It’s nice, this is something that has been very tough for me. I often have too much respect for these guys, which is part of the culture, and I’m proud of that, but it’s a little bit in the way when you have to play them.”

The Belgian reached the quarter-final last year, but lost in straight sets against Novak Djokovic.

Bergs continued: “I think I had a great moment last year here against Djokovic, I was definitely playing the name, not the guy. The more experience you have practising and playing the matches, the more it becomes the new standard a little bit on the Tour.

“To have this moment, it’s really a relief. Like okay, I feel like now I can win against those guys. I can play against them I can win against them. It’s a matter of also staying in the process and trying to be better all the time. That’s the only way to do it, step by step.”

title: Wuhan Open withdrawal list: 15 WTA stars out as Zheng Qinwen and two Grand Slam winners also pull out
article_text:
The 2026 Wuhan Open has been dealt another couple of blows as Chinese hero Zheng Qinwen has joined the list of big-name players to pull out of the WTA 1000 event.

Just hours after delighting her fans by winning her maiden WTA 1000 title, the China Open on home soil in Beijing, Zheng confirmed that she won’t feature in the second leg of the double-header in Wuhan.

“I’m very sorry to share that I will be withdrawing from this year’s Wuhan Open,” she said in a statement. “Wuhan is where my tennis dream began, and the Wuhan Open is also where I made my breakthrough at the WTA 1000 level. I have always looked forward to competing in front of my hometown fans.

“Since returning from injury … I have played a demanding stretch of tennis over the past month and a half, competing at the US Open, the Billie Jean King Cup, and the China Open.

“My body is feeling very fatigued after this intense run of matches.”

The 2024 Australian Open runner-up has been in brilliant form recently as, after dropping out of the top 100 in the WTA Rankings, she bounced back by reaching the quarter-finals of the US Open after coming through qualifying.

She followed it up with a title run at the China Open with her latest result helping her to return to the top 30 in the rankings.

Zheng defeated new world No 3 Mirra Andreeva in straight sets on Sunday and the reigning French Open champion will also not feature in Wuhan as she also cited fatigue after her run to the final in Beijing.

Those withdrawals came not long after reigning Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova withdrew due to a calf injury.

Andreeva and Noskova’s no shows led to a change in the draw as Andreeva was seeded third and had a bye into the second round, but she will now be replaced by Iva Jovic on Line 17 with the American heading into the second round.
