title: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season
article_text:
Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European tour in 2027.

The European tour, which is sponsored by DP World, said players must "make a choice" regarding where they play - a significantly tougher stance than in recent seasons.

Only players who are members of the DP World Tour can play for Europe in the Ryder Cup.

Deadlines for both tours are in the next five weeks, though there remains uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf's future despite it securing a possible $300m in funding as it attempts to restructure.

"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport.

"We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by.

"Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."

In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.

However, players will be asked to disclose which tours they intend to play on for next year, and their answer will be taken into account when deciding on their membership.

About 15 LIV players - including Rahm, Hatton, Victor Perez and Tom McKibbin - have "status" with the DP World Tour, meaning they have eligibility under one of the membership categories.

Other LIV players, like Joaquin Niemann and Thomas Pieters, do not have such status so would either need to go through qualifying school or sign agreements with the DP World Tour by which they would receive invitations to a set number of tournaments.

However, those agreements would only be available to players who were not part of LIV in the future.

BBC Sport has been told the DP World Tour will not accept membership from anyone intending to play on what is being called LIV 2.0.

If players did not disclose their intention to play LIV and went on to do so, that would be considered grounds on which to have their membership terminated.

LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September as it attempted to restructure, following the withdrawal of its multi-billion dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Last week, it announced it had secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.

While the DP World Tour agreed to grant conditional releases with nine players this season, it is understood the change for 2027 is predominantly down to LIV offering players equity in future and a feeling this is incompatible with the European tour being a members organisation.

However, it also comes at a time when the DP World Tour's strategic alliance with the PGA Tour is being negotiated, so the move likely reflects a desire to put itself in the best position possible in those discussions.

Players will have until 16 November to sign up to the DP World Tour for next year.

Under the terms of its court-supervised restructuring process, LIV Golf needs to sign players up by 25 October.

Ted Goldthorpe, head of BC Partners Credit, told BBC Sport last week he was "confident" LIV would have a "critical mass" of players.

But since then two-time major winner Rahm has said he will not continue playing on the LIV tour.

Lawyers representing a number of other players, including fellow major winners Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith, sought clarification from the court that rejection of contracts would equate to "termination", enabling players to hold discussions with third parties about their futures.

Richard Bland is currently the only player to have stated publicly a desire to play on LIV 2.0.

However, Perez indicated last month he hoped there would be a future for the league.

title: Forrest earns major invites with Spanish Open win
article_text:
Scotland's Grant Forrest held off a charge from home favourite Eugenio Chacarra to win the Spanish Open and book a spot at The Open and the Masters next year.

With Chacarra in the clubhouse at 13 under, Forrest and playing partner Victor Perez needed to make birdies at the 18th to go above the Spaniard.

Both players' drives nestled down in the greenside rough on the 322-yard par four, and after Perez's birdie putt drifted past the hole, Forrest sunk his to seal his third DP World Tour title and a first professional win outside Scotland.

"I'm in pure shock just now," Forrest said. "It's been such a tough year. I've got good memories of this course and this tournament. To do it is unbelievable.

"It was tough. I wasn't too sure what other groups were doing. It was a matter of staying in it. I dug in so well.

"That's fairytale stuff, I've played two Opens and to be going to Augusta, I just can't get my head round it. You can have a great career in this game and never get to go to Augusta, so I cannot believe it."

Going into the final round in a share of the lead with England's Joe Dean on 13 under, Forrest birdied the fourth, but made bogeys at three, six and eight as he dropped two shots off the top.

However, Forrest showed excellent resilience and moved back into a share of the lead as he started his back nine with three birdies and a bogey in five holes.

And he got the job done with a tidy up-and-down at the last to card a closing one-under 70 and take home the £480,000 first prize.

title: DP World Tour bans LIV Golf players for 2027, ending their Ryder Cup eligibility
article_text:
Whatever becomes of LIV Golf 2.0, the DP World Tour has decided it won’t let those who compete in the rebel circuit’s new version have it both ways. In a statement to BBC Sport, DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings said the European circuit, which had previously reached agreements with LIV players to allow them into its tournaments, will no longer do so in 2027, effectively banning them from playing.

“Players need to make a choice,” Kinnings told BBC Sport. “We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by. Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour.”

The DP World Tour had reached agreements that included granting conditional releases to LIV players in part to allow players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton to maintain their Ryder Cup eligibility. The DP World Tour oversees the European team, like the PGA of America oversees the American side. This détente included Hatton and Rahm agreeing earlier this year to a settlement that required them to pay their outstanding fines for competing in the formerly Saudi-backed league in exchange for European Tour eligibility. Those deals applied only to the 2026 season. With LIV struggling to survive as it goes through bankruptcy in hopes of reinventing itself, the DP World Tour will no longer let LIV players have their cake and eat it too.

The deadline to apply for membership on the DP World Tour is Nov. 16, while the deadline for players to commit to LIV Golf 2.0 is Oct. 25. The DP World Tour will now ask players to disclose which tours they intend to play in 2027, and that will be taken into account when deciding if they are to be given membership on the European circuit. Players like Rahm, Hatton, and Tom McKibbin, who played on LIV but also had “status” on the DP World Tour under certain categories, will no longer be allowed to double-dip. Players like Joaquin Niemann don’t have status and would need to either go through DP World Tour Qualifying School or strike a deal with the DP World Tour to play a set number of events on sponsor invitations. Such deals would also be available only to players not playing on LIV 2.0. If a player signs a deal with the DP World Tour and also tries to play on LIV, their membership or contract would be terminated.

The DP World Tour’s ban comes as it renegotiates its alliance with the PGA Tour. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp has not yet said when, if or how he will allow defectors to return to the PGA Tour.

LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September as it looks to restructure after the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund announced it was withdrawing funding from the league after the 2026 season. Last week, LIV and its new investor, BC Partners, formalized a restructuring support agreement under which the London-based private equity firm will fund LIV 2.0. BC Partners announced an “initial committed investment” as part of a targeted $300 million in cumulative financing to help the league, which the court must approve.

A day after the RSA was filed, Rahm’s attorney told a New Jersey bankruptcy court that the two-time major winner will not be part of LIV 2.0. In the days since Rahm’s intentions were made clear, Adrian Meronk and David Puig have also announced they won’t be taking part in the reboot. Hatton has not yet said publicly what he plans to do. Sergio Garcia’s representation asked the court for clarity on his LIV contract and subsequently had it terminated.

Rahm and Hatton are key members of the European side, which will look to win its third Ryder Cup in a row next September. Garcia has said he told captain Luke Donald that he plans to try to make the team but would also be interested in an assistant captaincy if he doesn’t. The DP World Tour’s decision to stop granting releases, ending any LIV players’ Ryder Cup eligibility, adds another obstacle for the breakaway league as it looks to retain talent and get its reboot off the ground.

At a London conference last week, BC Partners credit head Ted Goldthorpe said he and his company are very “committed” to LIV Golf and expect to have a “critical mass” of players by the Oct. 25 deadline. While many, including the PIF, have wondered if BC Partners is only interested in LIV for the purposes of a tax write-off, Goldthorpe said that “wasn’t the driving force behind the investment.”

The next hearing in LIV”s bankruptcy case will take place on Wednesday, Oct. 14.

title: 'I'm dejected': Late bogeys cost promising pro PGA Tour card
article_text:
Sunday saw a host of young and journeyman pros alike experience the highlight of their careers: earning PGA Tour cards at the 2026 Korn Ferry Tour Championship.

As happens every year, heartwarming tales about players’ big achievements abound. But there is another side to the story: the other pros who just missed out on their Tour cards.

On Sunday, the pain that group felt was best exemplified by Cole Hammer.

The 27-year-old Texas pro narrowly lost his grasp on his own Tour card with a poor final round on Sunday. But instead of fleeing the course as fast as he could, a “dejected” Hammer faced the cameras and opened up about his unfortunate fate. In the process, he showed a hard-earned perspective that should serve him well as he continues his pro career.

At the end of the Korn Ferry Tour Championship, the top 20 players in the season-long standings earn their PGA Tour cards for the next season.

Heading into last week’s event, Hammer was the lucky bubble boy, sitting in the all-important 20th position in the standings. It had been a long time coming for the former star amateur.

Hammer played his college golf at the University of Texas, where he helped his team to an NCAA title in 2022. A former U.S. Amateur Four-Ball champion, Hammer was named the best amateur in the world back in 2019.

Hammer has played sporadically on the PGA Tour, before and after turning pro in 2022. In the 2022-23 season, he made 10 PGA Tour starts, earning his only career top-10 finish, a T5 at the 2022 RSM Classic.

But without a PGA Tour card, Hammer has spent most of his pro career on the Korn Ferry Tour. In three previous full Korn Ferry Tour seasons, Hammer’s best finish in the season-long standings was 65th.

The 2026 season has been a different story. Three early T4s followed by a T2 at the Utah Championship, where he lost in a five-way playoff, moved Hammer to 20th in the KFT standings.

He briefly fell out of Tour card contention. Then in September Hammer finished T6 and T7 in back-to-back KFT events to jump to 18th in the standings, before a T53 at last week’s Compliance Solutions Championship dropped him back to 20th.

With a PGA Tour card on the line at the Korn Ferry Tour Championship, he opened last week’s event with a disappointing 72, but then charged back up the leaderboard with a 67 on Friday and a 69 on Saturday. With one more solid round, Hammer could at last earn his PGA Tour card for the first time.

But in the final round of the final event of the season, Hammer’s luck would run out. Five Sunday bogeys, including one on his second-to-last hole, dashed Hammer’s hopes.

By day’s end, he signed for a two-over 73 to finish the tournament T43. In the process, Hammer fell from 20th to 22nd in the final standings, surrendering his claim to a PGA Tour card for next year.

Immediately after his round, Hammer did a one-on-one interview posted on the Korn Ferry Tour’s social channels. He admitted he was “bummed” at the result and said his ball striking had ultimately betrayed him.

“It was a battle all day, I didn’t have it. I really didn’t have anything out there at all except my putter. And that can only bail you out so much,” Hammer said after his round. “And it just… bad ball striking caught up to me, and, yeah, I’m a little bummed out right now.”

He then explained that he was feeling good until his momentum was zapped by back-to-back bogeys on his eighth and ninth holes of the day.

“I got off to a decent start and got to my 8th hole which is No. 17 and made a bad bogey, and then had a 9-iron from the middle of the fairway on 18 and bogeyed there as well. And it just lost all my momentum,” Hammer explained.

He continued: “I was maybe a couple good holes away from kind of breaking it open and giving myself a little cushion on the back nine. And it just didn’t happen. I didn’t hit the shots I needed to. And so, I mean, what can I do?”

With Hammer dropping to 22nd, David Lamb, who had begun the week in 23rd, finished in 20th to earn the final PGA Tour card up for grabs.

Hammer positive despite Tour card disappointment: ‘I just believe in myself. It’s been a fun journey’

But it wasn’t all doom and gloom. While Hammer was honest about his major disappointment, he also acknowledged a lot of positives he took from the day.

Despite now having to play another season on the Korn Ferry Tour, Hammer affirmed that he still “believed” in himself and called his years-long quest for a PGA Tour card a “fun journey.”

“Having a chance at a PGA Tour card today was a pretty cool experience, and, yeah, I’m dejected right now, and I’m sure I will be for a while, but I just believe in myself,” Hammer said on Sunday. “It’s been a fun journey. It’s been five or six years of learning.”

While he admitted that he thought he was going to pull through and earn his Tour card on Sunday, he’s not getting down on himself. Instead, he’s excited about the future.

title: Tour Confidential: Can LIV Golf survive without Jon Rahm?
article_text:
Check in every week for the unfiltered opinions of our writers and editors as they break down the hottest topics in the sport, and join the conversation by tweeting us at @golf_com. This week, we discuss Jon Rahm’s decision to decline LIV 2.0 and what the PGA Tour should do about it.

Jon Rahm is officially out of LIV Golf 2.0, his lawyer announced last week, a major blow to the league that’s already treading water after recently filing for bankruptcy. With already few stars, can LIV Golf survive without Rahm on board?

Josh Berhow, managing editor (@Josh_Berhow): Any league is only as strong as its stars, so Rahm leaving is obviously a massive loss. You need these tentpoles to market your product and bring in eyeballs, and LIV already has so few of them. Rahm is kind of like a Jenga piece — pulling his block alone doesn’t bring down the whole tower, but pull a few more blocks and things can come crashing down in a hurry.

Sean Zak, senior writer: Just because it continues doesn’t necessarily mean much. But losing Rahm is absolutely massive, even if it was expected. He was one of two LIV golfers the world cared about during majors. He was one of only a few LIV golfers who contended in majors. The league can survive in an extremely trimmed-down derivative form, which it has planned to do for the last few months. But it all feels a bit rudderless while stuck in bankruptcy court.

Zephyr Melton, associate game-improvement editor (@zephyrmelton): Survive in terms of continuing to stage professional golf tournaments? Likely yes. Survive in terms of being a major player in the global golf landscape? No chance. Without the names they are losing, the tour is no different than the Sunshine Tour or Challenge Tour.

A couple other Spaniards — Sergio Garcia and David Puig — also appear out at LIV, although the Rahm news was certainly the headliner. If you’re a LIV player right now with options, what are you thinking? Is Rahm’s departure the start of an exodus?

Berhow: There are a lot of LIV players who don’t have as many options, so their spot in the league feels more secure. But they aren’t the ones you really have to worry about. There’s just a handful you really need to watch. What’s Joaquin Niemann thinking? What about Tyrrell Hatton? And, most importantly, how does Rahm leaving affect Bryson DeChambeau’s decision? Bryson is more marketable than Rahm, and now all eyes are on him and what he might decide to do. He holds a lot of power when it comes to LIV’s future, but ironically not so much with the PGA Tour, which Bryson needs more than it needs Bryson.

Zak: Rahm’s a precedent, which is all LIV has ever really been. Phil Mickelson set the precedent by committing early on. So did Dustin Johnson. This is a precedent in the opposite direction. I’m not sure Rahm’s inclusion matters too much to, say, Cameron Smith, but I think a lot of golf fans wish it mattered to Cameron Smith. Which is to say, if a league with only a handful of top players loses its best player, it really should inspire others to follow his path. I’ll just wait and watch, much like I did in the summer of ‘22.

Melton: I’d expect those without solid status elsewhere to stay, but for those who can secure a soft landing, LIV will be in the rearview mirror. They already cashed in on their payday. No reason to stick around.

What does the PGA Tour, and CEO Brian Rolapp, do now? Rahm didn’t accept the deal that was offered to Brooks Koepka via the Returning Member Program, and Rolapp has not sounded keen on rolling out the red carpet for LIV players who wish to return. But should he make an exception for Rahm? Is the one-year suspension fair? What do you think will and should happen?

Berhow: Rolapp has said the Returning Member Program had an expiration date, and I think it would be a terrible look to bring back Rahm immediately and with only a few slaps on the wrist. Yes, he would make the PGA Tour stronger. (I want Scottie and Rory battling Rahm more often just like everyone else.) But he also decided to take hundreds of millions of dollars and go to a league that was trying to bury the other. I think a one-year suspension, where we see Rahm on the DP World Tour and at majors, at a minimum, is sufficient. And if the penalty is something like that, and you are a player on the PGA Tour, are you OK with that? I’d still have a bad taste in my mouth.

Zak: I actually think Rolapp shouldn’t make any exemption for anyone. There’s a clear pathway through the DP World Tour. If Rolapp wants to widen it a touch, in to the 2028 Championship Series, now would be the time — before those pathways have all been decided — to slip some access through without many people noticing. That would give him a lot of credit with the 150 or so other players who he’s asking to fight for their future next year. Why shouldn’t Rahm have to fight just as hard, or harder?

Melton: I agree with Zak. If you can play your way back, fine. But there should be no special treatment for those who passed up their opportunity to come back in the past. The Tour has proven it can survive without them — and will continue to.

title: Teenage phenom earns Tour card, sets record the hard way
article_text:
Sunday may not have been the exact result 19-year-old Blades Brown was looking for — a fourth 54-hole lead squandered — but it ultimately saw him earn what he wanted next: a season full of starts on the PGA Tour.

Brown is well known to this point, partly due to his golfy name and partly due to his impressive game. He turned pro at just 17 and has played on the Korn Ferry Tour much of the last two seasons, occasionally sprinkling in some starts on the PGA Tour. He flashed in moments this summer, never quite getting across the line for a win, but the floor has been extremely high. He’s made 16 of 18 cuts and finished in the top 10 five times.

What that all means is — despite a second-place finish in Sunday’s final KFT event — Brown will be all over your television on the PGA Tour next spring. He’ll still be 19 then, a reminder that he has now set the record for youngest player to earn a Tour card via graduation from the KFT.

Before he truly got into contention this weekend, Brown was asked if his accomplishments arriving at such a young age really resonate with him.

“I mean, a little bit,” he admitted. “One thing I know is I always tell my dad the golf ball doesn’t care how old I am. The golf ball doesn’t know if you’re 60 years old or 19 years old, so I would say that.”

You may hear Brown issue that quote a few more times at the beginning of 2027. He’ll be a teenager until next year’s PGA Championship.

Brown finished ninth in the season-long Korn Ferry Tour race, which means he’ll have decent status when 2027 begins. He may have to stay patient through the early-season tournaments, as ninth on KFT will put him right on the border of alternate status into a handful of the more desired west coast events, like the Phoenix Open. But if we’ve learned anything about him to this point, it’s that he’s very comfy playing a bunch of golf.

In between his 18 KFT starts in 2026, Brown jumped over for 11 starts on the PGA Tour, making nine cuts and finishing in the top 20 seven times. He even earned Special Temporary Membership on Tour for the rest of the season, but he opted to spend more time chasing the path via its feeder tour. What feels most clear from all of that is his floor — it’s very high. What he gets to show us know is what the ceiling looks like.

title: How Bernhard Langer unintentionally taught future pro important lesson
article_text:
Alistair Docherty’s first golf memory provided a couple of valuable lessons. The 32-year-old pro, who will be a PGA Tour card-holder for the first time come 2027, joined this week’s GOLF Subpar podcast and explained how a trip to Sahalee Country Club played a key role in his life.

Sahalee is a private country club in Sammamish, Wash., just outside of Seattle, and in 2010 it hosted the U.S. Senior Open. (It was also home to the 1998 PGA Championship, won by Vijay Singh.) But in 2010, Docherty attended the U.S. Senior Open with his father, and they found a spot to sit by the 10th tee.

That’s when Bernhard Langer came through — and promptly fired his tee shot into one of the many evergreens on the famously tree-lined golf course.

“I looked at my dad and I’m like, ‘Wow, pros hit bad shots too,'” Docherty said. But the best players in the world hitting bad shots wasn’t the main takeaway, it was what happened next. “I’m like, ‘What’s going to happen now?’ Well, he won that week. So a bad shot doesn’t really determine the outcome. … And to be fair, if anyone’s been up to Sahalee, it’s called Sah-hallway for a reason.”

title: 'Fairytale stuff': Pro's hard year ends with ticket to 2027 Masters
article_text:
Eleven years ago, Grant Forrest had a ticket to the Masters in his grasp. Then a budding Scottish amateur star, Forrest reached the finals of the 2015 Amateur Championship. A win meant not only one of amateur golf’s biggest prizes but also a trip to Magnolia Lane. But a 4&2 loss to Romain Langasque meant Forrest’s Augusta National dream would have to wait.

The wait wasn’t expected to be long. Forrest made the 2015 Walker Cup team and was expected to be one of Europe’s bright young stars. But golf had other plans. Forrest turned pro and worked his way up from the Challenge Tour to the DP World Tour, finally reaching the top European circuit in 2019. His first DP World Tour win arrived at the 2021 Hero Open. His next came four years later at the 2025 Nexo Championship. Along the way, Forrest played in two Open Championships and one U.S. Open, but never played well enough to reach Augusta National.

It seemed unlikely that Forrest would reach golf’s hallowed grounds in 2027. His DP World Tour season has been one of the toughest of his pro career. He entered this week’s Open de España presented by Madrid having posted just one top-10 and three top-20s on the season. His best finish was a T7 at the Bahrain Championship in January. He hadn’t finished better than 63rd since June.

It was a lost year for Forrest, but he still had a chance to do something special this week in Madrid. In golf, all it takes is four good rounds to change everything.

He opened with rounds of 66-66-67 to share the 54-hole lead with Joe Dean. A triumphant Sunday would mark his first DP World Tour win away from Scottish soil and earn him spots in the 2027 Masters and Open Championship. But Forrest struggled out of the gate on Sunday, going out in 2-over 38 as Eugenio Chacarra and Victor Perez rose up the leaderboard. But resilience has been the theme of a trying season for Forrest, so after another bogey at the 11th, he buckled down to give himself a chance at the win of a lifetime. He birdied 13 and 14 to climb into a tie for the lead and arrived at the driveable par-4 18th in a three-way tie atop the board with Perez and Chacarra, who had already posted 13 under.

Forrest’s drive nestled in the greenside rough right next to Perez’s tee ball. Forrest played his chip to five feet, and when Perez missed a nine-foot birdie attempt, the door opened for Grant Forrest to finally get to Augusta National — a chance he took when he calmly rolled in his winning birdie putt to get to 14 under and claim the title.

“It’s fairytale stuff,” Forrest said of earning spots in the Masters and Open at St. Andrews. “To be going to Augusta, I can’t get my head around it. I was close in the Amateur Championship 11 years ago now. But you can have a great career in this game and never get to go to Augusta, so I just — I cannot believe it.

Forrest spent his entire 2026 in the wilderness, struggling to find his game but vowing to grind it out. In golf, things are rarely as good or as bad as they seem. There was little reason to expect it all to come together this week in Spain, and things lo looked bleak at points on Sunday as he slid down the leaderboard. But with a rare opportunity in front of him, Forrest steadied the ship and played well enough to reach a place he’s always wanted his game to take him.

“It was tough,” Forrest said. “It was just a matter of keeping yourself in it. I think we did that really well. Couple of nice putts at the right time and just dug in there so well despite a couple of frustrating things.

“I’m in shock, honestly,” Forrest added, “Just pure shock. It has been such a tough year. I just have not played well. Not played well at all… To walk away with a win is just unbelievable.”

title: 2026 Baycurrent Classic money: Here’s how much every player made
article_text:
Sunday at Yokohama Country Club began with a packed leaderboard and a world of possibilities. It ended with Michael Brennan holding off Jacob Bridgeman and Keith Mitchell to win the Baycurrent Classic, his third PGA Tour title in 12 months.

“Unbelievable. It was an unbelievable week. Japan was spectacular, the fans were amazing this week,” Brennan said after his win.

Mitchell, who is still searching for his first win since the 2019 Honda Classic, took the lead on the front nine with three birdies and an eagle. But he dropped shots at Nos. 9 and 12, leaving him one shot behind Brennan coming down the stretch. Mitchell striped his tee shot on 18 and left himself a 10-foot birdie putt to tie Brennan at 16 under, but he couldn’t get it to fall.

“I felt like every part of my game held up except a couple putts here and there,” Mitchell said after his T2 finish. “Probably hit the best two shots in my life, that’s stuff to say, but the tee shot on 18 and the 7-iron on 18 were as good as I got. Unfortunately, the putt wasn’t as good as I got. So if I can give it the same as the long shots, maybe we’re having a different conversation.”

Bridgeman, who won the Biltmore Championship last month, also had a chance to catch Brennan, but he missed a 5-foot birdie putt on 17 and finished T2 with Mitchell.

“Was able to make some putts at important times that I needed; that one on 17 is going to sting a little bit,” Bridgeman said.

Defending champion Xander Schauffele shot a final-round 4-under 67 to finish T4 with Brian Harman, Jordan Smith, Ryan Gerard and Stephan Jaeger.

“I definitely played good enough golf to win this tournament,” Schauffele said.

title: These top-selling training aids improve common swing ailments — and make great gifts!
article_text:
If you’re looking for the ultimate golf gift, it’s tough to argue with the wow factor of an improved golf game. A lower handicap is truly the gift that keeps on giving! However, giving game-improvement products can be a delicate endeavor. Nobody wants to be told they’re deficient in any area of the game, and the holidays probably aren’t the ideal time to poke at potentially sore feelings.

But for open-minded giftees, we love the idea of wrapping up a tried-and-true training aid. Here at GOLF, we’re always on the lookout for the latest and greatest tools to help you achieve your performance goals. Sharing is caring! So if you’re looking for some gift-giving inspiration on the training aid front, we’ve rounded up five best-selling products below, along with some commentary on what makes them great. Cheers to the start of the holiday shopping season — and better golf in 2027!

This low-cost grip trainer is beloved by Scottie Scheffler — and makes a great stocking stuffer.

“The fundamentals may not be the most exciting things to work on, but when they are in working order, playing consistent golf becomes much easier,” wrote associate game-improvement editor Zephyr Melton. “You may not swing like Scheffler with a grip trainer, but at least you can practice like him.”

“I can see why this product went viral a few years ago,” said game-improvement editor Maddi MacClurg. “The Eagle Mat Pro doesn’t overcomplicate things — it just shows you what’s happening at impact and lets you work from there. For me, it turned practice into something more focused, fun and effective.”

The Pressure Plate teaches you to load your weight onto your lead side before impact, resulting in better contact and ball compression. Practicing with the Pressure Plate will help you understand the importance of swing sequence, the right time to transition your weight and how to maximize ground forces to hit more powerful shots.

“Swinging with a resistance band around my legs was a great way to train my body to swing without early extending,” said MacClurg. “This is a great drill to practice on the range when you are actually hitting golf balls. After a while, you can take the band off and try to maintain that feel when you swing. If you can continue to feel that pressure on the outside of your legs, you will stabilize your core and make it difficult to early extend.”

“For golfers who struggle with alignment, setup or unwanted movement, the Why Golf Alignment Mirror is a smart way to check your swing,” said MacClurg. “It helped me become more aware of my tendencies and, more importantly, gave me a simpler way to work on them.”

title: Man City's Omar Marmoush fined over uninsured McLaren
article_text:
Tottenham striker Omar Marmoush has been fined after his McLaren supercar was found to be uninsured and not declared off the road.

The 27-year-old, who joined Spurs on loan from Manchester City in August, was found guilty at Teesside Magistrates' Court on 5 October.

He was fined £220 and ordered to pay £100 in costs and an £88 victim surcharge, according to the Press Association (PA).

The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) brought the prosecution after Marmoush failed to pay a fixed penalty issued in June.

Court papers show the footballer was issued with the penalty on 17 June after officials discovered his McLaren 720S, worth an estimated £250,000, was uninsured and had not been declared off the road.

The DVLA attempted to contact Marmoush at an apartment in Manchester city centre where he had been living before his move to London.

The case was dealt with under the Single Justice Procedure, which allows magistrates to deal with certain criminal cases behind closed doors without a conventional court hearing.

Marmoush did not enter a plea or respond to the papers sent to him by the DVLA.

Marmoush's move to Tottenham, announced at the end of August, includes an obligation for the club to buy him for £60m at the end of the season.

The Egyptian player was part of his country's World Cup squad this summer; he scored 10 goals for Manchester City after joining the club in January 2025.

title: The 'Kane-esque' striker Spurs may regret letting go
article_text:
Leaping high, six yards out, to nod in Tommy Conway's cross from the left wing, Will Lankshear notched his ninth goal in 12 games for Middlesbrough.

It is that positioning, finishing and poacher's instinct, earning Boro a 1-0 win against Wolves on Saturday, that has made Lankshear an instant hit at Riverside Stadium – and a cause of lament at Tottenham Hotspur.

Lankshear joined Boro from Spurs in the summer on a five-year contract in a deal that could rise to a club record buy of £20m.

Since then, he has scored as many goals in all competitions as Spurs' combined team. His old side, despite snatching a draw at Manchester United a few hours after Lankshear's latest winner, remain in the Premier League relegation zone while Boro sit in the Championship's automatic promotion places.

Dominic Solanke's last-minute goal at Old Trafford was the first league goal scored by a Tottenham forward in five months.

It is enough to make Spurs fans despair.

"A lot of fans are wondering why he was sold," Ali Speechly, co-chair of the Women of the Lane supporters' group, told BBC Sport.

"It was likely to do with money - his sell-on price is relatively high, so let's cash in on him.

"I was definitely disappointed. Given how badly we have started this season, as a fan it feels like the wrong decision."

Amid a multi-million pound summer splurge, Spurs allowed Lankshear to leave for an initial fee worth about £10m, with an additional £10m due in add-ons based on various clauses.

Boro saw off competition around the Championship, and in Europe, to sign the 21-year-old who impressed at Oxford United in the second tier last season, scoring 12 league goals on loan for a relegated side.

Good form for a young player, but not so compelling he had to go straight into the Spurs first team.

"If you are a young kid at a club where you are not getting any first-team football and you get the opportunity to go and play men's football, you should go," former Spurs goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Sport.

"The academies are great and Premier League 2 is a great feeder for the first team, but if you are 21, 22 or 23 and still mostly playing in the under-23s then you have missed the boat.

"Getting first-team football is the best grounding you can get for a young footballer, getting the opportunity to play in the first team, regardless of what league it is. Will has been given this opportunity, and he is taking it."

Lankshear scored 23 goals for Tottenham's U23 team in the 2023–24 Premier League 2 season and played for the senior side in the 2024-25 Europa League campaign – most notably scoring then getting sent off against Galatasaray.

But amid a churn of players and managers at Spurs, he has moved on – and Boro fans couldn't be happier.

Middlesbrough have built a reputation in recent years of providing a springboard for promising youngsters. Most notably, Morgan Rogers spent six months at Riverside Stadium before joining Aston Villa, and the rest is history.

Not only that, but Boro - who missed out on promotion last season after scoring only once in three play-off games - badly needed a skilful, physical presence who could finish the multitude of chances made by Kim Hellberg's creative but blunt side.

"Boro was a team that made a boatload of chances, and he knew he would be able to get on the end of them," BBC Tees commentator Mark Drury told BBC Sport.

"But what people have been impressed with is his instinctive finishing - one touch, just being in the right place. It's simple but not a lot of people know how to be there at the right time, to give yourself the highest percentage chance.

"He's taller and stockier than he might look from the sidelines, and he is only 21. He seems to have the all-round package - good with both feet and in the air."

A 6ft 2in English striker with a deadly finishing touch, who came through at Spurs before learning his trade in the Football League. Remind you of anyone?

"I can understand the comparisons with Harry Kane," said Robinson. "He has headed down a similar career path to Harry and, physically, he has a similar stature as well.

"Like Kane, he looks like a player who is developing a little later, compared to others who are Premier League regulars before the end of their teens.

"You look at him and the career path he is on; it is a very similar one to the one Harry Kane has been on, and that is a big positive. There is no substitute for playing in the first team somewhere, regardless of what level you are playing at."

Like Kane, Lankshear also had early career setbacks. Initially at Arsenal's academy, he was released and signed with Sheffield United before being picked up by Spurs for £2m when he was 17.

He also had hit-and-miss loan spells. An unremarkable stint at West Brom was followed by a more fruitful spell with Oxford.

"Harry Kane didn't always have brilliantly successful loan spells, they are not always a marker of a player," says Speechly.

"He didn't do anything remarkable, but it is unfortunate as we are not scoring goals. It is painful to see.

"I don't think we will ever get another Kane, but there are definitely similarities. He is a real poacher and has a strong work ethic. It is very Kane-esque."

title: De Zerbi has his Pochettino moment and the strange decision during Tottenham's draw at Man United
article_text:
It started with a kiss. Well technically it started with a push and then a coming together of heads.

Whatever it started with, the script finally ended differently for Tottenham Hotspur. The familiar tale this season of playing well, failing to take chances and coming away with nothing did not come to pass.

It had looked like it was heading that way, Spurs dominant in the first half with the ball and creating big chances for Dominic Solanke at the start of both periods and Conor Gallagher before the interval.

They did not play like the away side at Old Trafford, producing some eye-catching moments of football with and without the ball, and for long periods the Manchester United fans among the 74,129-strong crowd were frustrated and left booing as the travelling Tottenham faithful, making their way up the country around various cancellations from Euston, sang loud and proud.

Yet again they could not put the ball into the net and one defensive lapse looked to have seen them off, Matheus Cunha allowed too much time to find Bryan Mbeumo, who was given space by Jan Paul van Hecke to turn and fire past Antonin Kinsky.

The spark - the word offered up by Roberto De Zerbi's translator Enrico Venturelli after the game - came five minutes later through a moment of madness by substitute Rodrigo Bentancur.

The Uruguayan and Jan Paul van Hecke had both launched into lunging challenges, Bentancur's the cleaner of the two if not more of a scissor motion. He got nowhere near Luke Shaw but the United defender took exception to it.

The 31-year-old ran over to the Spurs midfielder off the ball and shoved him aggressively to the floor. The rules over shoving when it comes to bookings or red cards are so interchangeable that you could interpret Shaw's action either way depending on your point of view.

FOLLOW OUR TOTTENHAM FB PAGE! Latest Spurs news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

It was Bentancur's reaction though that changed the course of the encounter as the furious 29-year-old leapt up and thrust his head towards Shaw's. For a moment they went head to head until the United man realised the benefit of being the one thrusted at rather than a fellow thrustee.

It sparked a melee between both sides with substitutes joining in and staff having to act as peacemakers, the Spurs players showing their unity in protecting their team-mate including newcomers like Tosin Adarabioyo.

It was daft from the experienced Tottenham midfielder and in a moment he became a Uruguayan nutter, leaving referee Stuart Attwell with little choice but to brandish the red card.

There was little dispute to be had with Attwell's call on this occasion other than quibbling whether Shaw should have gone as well.

The same could not be said earlier in the second half during a bizarre moment when the referee allowed play to continue after the home side had taken the ball at least 3ft over the touchline behind the Spurs goal before being allowed to play on and fire the ball into the net.

The referee was stood closer to the moment than anyone, yet had to rely on his official to raise his flag. There's a case nowadays, rightly or wrongly, for letting moments run, for VAR to then referee the game but this stirred echoes of Pedro Mendes' goal that never was in that same arena as it was so far over the line.

There was not much argument over Bentancur's exit though, his first dismissal in a league game since May 2021 when he was sent off for Juventus against Inter. He became the first Spurs player to be red-carded as a substitute in the Premier League since Lucas Moura in April 2023 against Everton.

Ultimately though, Bentancur and Attwell's intervention on Saturday night sparked Spurs back to life, with Harry Maguire waving him goodbye, after a little spell of feeling sorry for themselves.

They pushed forward with 10 men, helped by the energy from the bench of James Maddison, Micky van de Ven, Omar Marmoush and eventually Mateus Fernandes.

The £85million Portuguese, yet to win De Zerbi's trust in his favoured central midfield position, was the catalyst for the 92nd minute equaliser. He was involved a couple of times in the move that led to Sandro Tonali curling in a perfect ball for Solanke to win his wrestling battle with Lisandro Martinez and deftly glance a header into the bottom right corner of the net.

The Old Trafford crowd were left stunned while the Spurs fans and players went wild. De Zerbi grabbed a spare ball by the touchline to his mouth and tried to take a hefty bite out of it as he screamed his delight.

After the game, football.london asked the Italian what he had said to Bentancur in the dressing room when he came off the pitch.

"I kissed Rodrigo, and I said thanks, because it's clear it's a mistake from Rodrigo, because it's not the right reaction in football, but now Tottenham needs to react," said the 47-year-old.

"Sometimes the reactions are not nice, not positive for the team, but I think in that moment, in 10 players, maybe we played with more courage, more energy and we changed the game.

"For a long time Tottenham played without this blood, this character, and I want it. Now I am the coach, I want to see this character every game, because Manchester United in the second half showed character, not just the quality. Just with the quality, we can't win the games.

title: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium breaks new record amid dramatic moment
article_text:
The Tottenham Hotspur Stadium broke their NFL crowd record during a dramatic encounter as the Jacksonville Jaguars secured a last-gasp win against the Philadelphia Eagles.

title: Rodrigo Bentancur agreement reached as Tottenham sent clear verdict on Man Utd red card
article_text:
Tottenham Hotspur have been given a clear verdict on Rodrigo Bentancur's red card against Manchester United after the Uruguay international was sent off for violent conduct.

The 29-year-old was sent off in the 78th minute, with United leading 1-0 thanks to a goal from Bryan Mbeumo. The Spurs man went flying into a tackle with Luke Shaw, before the defender reacted by pushing Bentancur.

The Spurs star appeared to headbutt the United full-back leaving the referee with little choice but to send him off. Fortunately for Roberto De Zerbi, Dominic Solanke popped up with a late equaliser to ensure a share of the spoils.

Speaking on Sky Sports Ref Watch about the incident, former referee Dermot Gallagher said: "I think it's a red card. I haven't spoken to many people who think it isn't. I just wonder if it could have been avoided.

"That tackle (Bentancur sliding on Shaw) has got to be punished. If you give a free-kick for that, it all goes away. What follows, though, I think it's a red card."

Jay Bothroyd agreed with the red card decision but said that both players were lucky to escape injury given their proximity to the advertising boards. Bothroyd said: "If Bentancur was closer to the sideline, he could have hurt himself, which would be dangerous play.

"That first Bentancur challenge should definitely be a booking. He's left the floor; he's out of control. It's an aggressive challenge.

"But by the letter of the law, as soon as you put your head in someone's face, you're gonna get a red card. But I would say Shaw's push is more dangerous than Bentancur's.

"If he's close enough to the touchline, he's flying into them boards. If any of those two challenges catch Shaw, he's coming off the pitch injured."

Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood says he can understand Shaw being aggravated by the challenges.

"Two tackles Shaw gets," Sherwood said on Sky Sports News. "Van Hecke comes in, gets away with that one, he jumps in. Then Bentancur comes in, I understand why Shaw got heated.

"I've got to say, has he got to wear shin pads? That might stop him getting injured. Is that not a yellow if you don't wear shin pads. He's got a couple of credit cards in his socks.

"If Shaw gets his toe to the ball there, he gets his leg broken."

title: Tottenham's fastest player in Manchester United draw might surprise you
article_text:
Tottenham took home a point from their dramatic 1-1 draw at Manchester United on Saturday and one of their summer signings logged the fastest sprint among the starters on the day.

Spurs dominated much of the first half in Manchester, frustrating the home fans with Conor Gallagher and Dominic Solanke thwarted by the keeper late in the first half before Solanke fired over inside the six-yard box early in the second period.

However, Roberto De Zerbi's men once again paid for their profligacy as they went behind in the 73rd minute. Matheus Cunha was allowed to find Bryan Mbeumo in the box and the former Brentford man had space to turn in front of Jan Paul van Hecke to strike a shot across Antonin Kinsky and into the net.

Matter got even worse five minutes later for the visitors when substitute Rodrigo Bentancur lost his head and thrust it into Luke Shaw's after the United defender shoved him to the ground. The red card was duly flourished by referee Stuart Attwell.

However, there was one late twist to come as Spurs found a leveller with 10 men in the 92nd minute as skipper for the day Solanke battled with Lisandro Martinez to head home Sandro Tonali's cross.

title: What Tottenham games Rodrigo Bentancur will miss as Premier League red card rules explained
article_text:
Rodrigo Bentancur will miss some huge Premier League games for Tottenham Hotspur due to suspension.

Roberto De Zerbi will be without Rodrigo Bentancur for three Premier League games, having been sent off for violent conduct during Tottenham Hotspur's hard-fought draw with Manchester United.

Unhappy with the challenge, Matheus Cunha charged over to smash the ball into the advertising board, but the Uruguay international managed to clear his lines just before his opposition arrived on the scene. By which point, Stewart Atwell had already blown his whistle, adjudging Bentancur to have just fouled Shaw.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the game, De Zerbi accepted that his player had made a 'mistake', but added that it sparked the reaction his side needed to salvage a point. He said: "I kissed Bentancur in the dressing room because we need this type of reaction, this character.

"Football is character. I liked the situation with the red card. We need at this moment the situation, not to bring a red card, but we need to not accept the defeat."

title: Lewis family increase Tottenham stake after £320m injection as Daniel Levy share shrinks
article_text:
The Lewis family have increased their stake in Tottenham after their recent £120million cash boost while former chairman Daniel Levy's slice of the club has shrunk.

The family, who own Spurs through investment company ENIC, have backed the Premier League club's attempts to transform to a more successful outfit with £320million injected into it over the past 12 months. Vivienne Lewis and her son-in-law Nick Beucher have taken a more active role in backing CEO Vinai Venkatesham and non-executive chairman Peter Charrington and the family have resisted interest from various parties in selling the club in the past couple of years.

The latest £120million injection for working capital has now officially increased the family's stake in Spurs to 89.06 per cent and after former chairman Levy did not take up the opportunity to match the cash boost with his own relative part of it, his slice in ENIC's pie at Tottenham has dwindled from being 29.8 per cent in October last year to 27.38 in June this year and now 25 per cent after two missed injection opportunities.

The north London club's investor relations page on their website now reads: "Of the total issued ordinary share capital of Tottenham Hotspur Limited, ENIC Sports, Inc. ownership is 89.06% (from 88.30%) to reflect shares allotted in September 2026. ENIC also owns the one THL convertible A share.

"Mr D Levy and certain members of his family are potential beneficiaries of discretionary trusts which ultimately own 25% of the share capital of ENIC. A discretionary trust of which certain members of Mr J Lewis's family are potential beneficiaries ultimately owns 75% of the share capital of ENIC."

FOLLOW OUR TOTTENHAM FB PAGE! Latest Spurs news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

Levy, who was chairman of Spurs for 24 years before being ousted in September last year by the Lewis family, has been linked since June with selling a large portion of his stake in ENIC to British Virgin Islands-based company Eight Sports Capital after they claimed the 64-year-old had signed a sale and purchase agreement with them.

Eight Sports Capital is spearheaded by two leading forces involved in two of the three rejected Spurs takeover bids last year. One is Wing-Fai Ng, the CEO of American entertainment company Triller, which owns Eight Sports. The other is tech entrepreneur Brooklyn Earick, who is the CEO of Eight Sports.

There was a third new person involved in Taiwanese billionaire Richard Tsai, who also owns Triller as well as Fubon Financial Holding Company, one of the largest financial conglomerates in Asia.

In May after Spurs had narrowly avoided relegation on the final day of the season, the Lewis family took the step of releasing their first ever message to the supporters.

"To the fans, As owners of 25 years, we have lived the highs and lows of Spurs with you," it read. "Finishing 17th this and last season does not reflect the stature or potential of this football club. We are bitterly disappointed and share your frustration. You, and we, expect more than this. We know this must never happen again.

"Our approach to running the club is, and has been, to trust the experts to do that, while backing them to be successful. The problems we found were deeper than we realised and were allowed to build over the last few years. We know that has eroded trust and we have to win that back. As owners, we take ultimate responsibility for the situation in which the club finds itself.

"We also take responsibility for rebuilding Spurs. Our ambition is to recapture the spirit of the club and bring back the excitement, the fearlessness and the bold football we have always felt defined us. That means football comes first. The Board and Executive team have laid out their plans to meet this ambition.

"This will require investment – in our teams, the academy, our backroom functions and more - and we are fully committed to this. We are not selling the club. We are all in. We are investing in it. You will see more of this in the coming months.

"We care deeply about Spurs. The rebuild the club needs, and you deserve, has begun. The change required is deep. It will take time and commitment, but change is happening. We know that actions will speak louder than words. The Lewis Family."

Spurs are yet to win in the Premier League in their opening six matches of the season under Roberto De Zerbi after a hefty summer transfer spend with 10 new arrivals but performances have improved as the new-look squad start to gel.

title: Alan Shearer lays into Tottenham star after Man Utd draw - 'Nowhere near good enough'

Alan Shearer has slammed Tottenham star Dominic Solanke's time at Spurs as 'nowhere near good enough' and said the forward is lacking confidence. The Premier League record goalscorer was not impressed with Solanke's impact against Manchester United.

The Lilywhites striker scored his first Premier League goal of the season against the Red Devils with a smart header after holding off Lisandro Martinez. But it was his wayward efforts throughout the match that frustrated Shearer.

One such effort in particular irked the former Newcastle star when Solanke was played through by Lucas Bergvall and awkwardly switched the ball with his right foot, killing the angle for his shot against Senne Lammens, and allowing the Belgian goalkeeper to make the save.

Shearer could not help but highlight Solanke's poor goalscoring record for Spurs after joining the club in a £55million deal. Solanke has netted 24 goals in 73 appearances for Spurs but has not hit double figures in the Premier League since leaving Bournemouth.

“It’s nowhere near good enough, only once in double figures when you consider the money they paid for him," Shearer said on Match of the Day.

“Just watch how awkward and how little confidence he has here, because of his desperation to get it onto the right foot here. Naturally, you move the ball out three yards on your left foot and hit it, if he had the belief.

“The lack of movement here: a goalscorer gets himself into the middle of the goal; where’s he going? When he says they need to be more clinical, he needs to be more clinical.”

"I wanted to make sure I kept getting as many as I can. I put one away so I’m thankful for that."

"When one player of us is in a difficult situation, all other players and staff and myself, we have to show, to be close with him, like a family, like a team, like a normal team."

title: HSBC: 80 years of banking on the UAE’s ambition
article_text:
On October 12, 1946, an international bank opened a small branch beside Dubai Creek. It was the first bank ever in Dubai. It was the result of a meeting between Frank Johnson, a manager of the Imperial Bank, with the late Sheikh Saeed Bin Maktoum Al Maktoum and his son, the late Sheikh Rashid Bin Saeed Al Maktoum. Johnson found rulers who already saw Dubai as a place the world would come to trade.

Eighty years on, that bank is HSBC Bank Middle East and the town it served is one of the world’s great centres of trade and finance.

The partnership in Dubai began with infrastructure. In 1954, the bank worked to help raise the loan for dredging the Creek, the project that opened the city to larger vessels and set the pattern for the port-led growth that followed. As the Emirates grew, so did our presence: Sharjah in 1953, Abu Dhabi in 1959, and in time branches serving customers across the UAE.

The credit for HSBC’s journey belongs to the UAE: to the vision of its leaders and the enterprise of its people. Our part has been to be a steady partner at every stage, and to connect the country’s ambitions to the rest of the world.

Each era has brought new expectations of what a bank should do. In 1984, we introduced the UAE’s first operational ATM. In 1990, we opened the first branch in Jebel Ali’s new banking complex, supporting the free zone that became a model for the region. Between 2004 and 2016, we advised on 10 of the independent water and power projects in Abu Dhabi, which helped to build the utilities that serve a growing population.

In 2016, we moved our place of incorporation and regional head office to the Dubai International Financial Centre. We have launched green mortgages, committed billions in lending to help UAE companies expand internationally, worked with the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on the region’s first digital bond and opened our first wealth centre in the Middle East at our flagship Jumeirah branch.

Across multiple sustainability partnerships, we have helped financial education programmes for young people and disadvantaged communities, we have supported initiatives for women returning to work and financed mangrove protection and restoration across the UAE’s coastline.

None of this happens without people. Generations of Emirati bankers began their careers with us and now lead across the country’s financial sector and beyond. Today, several of our senior executives, including the HSBC UAE CEO and me, as Chairman, are proud Emiratis in this journey. The exchange also runs both ways: many of HSBC’s senior leaders around the world, including our current Group CEO, spent their formative years in the UAE, learning what it means to bank a country that moves at this pace.

Anniversaries call on us to reflect on the past but in an organisation, with a culture and environment such as HSBC UAE, we look forward. What does a business need to do today to still be trading in 2106? We are asking ourselves, and our clients, that question as we mark this milestone.

For 80 years we have answered it consistently: stay open, invest ahead of need and build connections with the world. Today, the country sits at the centre of corridors linking Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas and its capital increasingly shapes markets far beyond its borders. Our role is to keep those corridors strong. That means helping UAE businesses grow internationally, bringing international capital to national priorities, and supporting the next generation of Emirati entrepreneurs and families as they build wealth that lasts.

In 1946, visionary leaders and a banker reached an agreement built on trust. That trust is still the foundation of everything we do. We are grateful to the UAE’s leadership, to our customers and to our colleagues past and present.

We look forward to the next 80 years together.

Players who sign up to play on a resurrected LIV Golf tour will be prohibited from competing on the DP World Tour or in the Ryder Cup, its European chiefs have said.

The rebel golf league has secured funding from BC Partners to exit bankruptcy proceedings after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund pulled its backing earlier this year.

Players including Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Cameron Smith have been offered equity in the new business and given until 25 October to pledge their continued allegiance. Rahm’s lawyer said he will not partake in the new season.

Any player who does will be banned from the Europe-based DP World Tour in a tougher policy than previous seasons, effectively ruling them out of Ryder Cup contention.

The tour’s chief, Guy Kinnings, told BBC Sport: “Players need to make a choice. We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by.

“Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour.”

The likes of Joaquin Niemann, who has picked up £60m in LIV Golf prize money, does not hold status with the DP World Tour and would instead need to go through qualifying school or find a way onto the PGA Tour.

As part of the bankruptcy deal, LIV Golf sought court authority to terminate existing player agreements, with this point set to be addressed at a wider hearing on Wednesday.

LIV chiefs are hoping for support from US president Donald Trump, having held numerous tournaments at his courses in the past.

“The Trump organisation has been tremendously supportive of LIV Golf,” CEO Scott O’Neil told the Sportico Invest London conference last week.

title: Golf: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season
article_text:
Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European tour in 2027.

The European tour, which is sponsored by DP World, said players must "make a choice" regarding where they play - a significantly tougher stance than in recent seasons.

Only players who are members of the DP World Tour can play for Europe in the Ryder Cup.

Deadlines for both tours are in the next five weeks, though there remains uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf's future despite it securing a possible $300m in funding as it attempts to restructure.

"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport.

"We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by.

"Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."

In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.

However, players will be asked to disclose which tours they intend to play on for next year, and their answer will be taken into account when deciding on their membership.

About 15 LIV players - including Rahm, Hatton, Victor Perez and Tom McKibbin - have "status" with the DP World Tour, meaning they have eligibility under one of the membership categories.

Other LIV players, like Joaquin Niemann and Thomas Pieters, do not have such status so would either need to go through qualifying school or sign agreements with the DP World Tour by which they would receive invitations to a set number of tournaments.

However, those agreements would only be available to players who were not part of LIV in the future.

BBC Sport has been told the DP World Tour will not accept membership from anyone intending to play on what is being called LIV 2.0.

If players did not disclose their intention to play LIV and went on to do so, that would be considered grounds on which to have their membership terminated.

LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September as it attempted to restructure, following the withdrawal of its multi-billion dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Last week, it announced it had secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.

While the DP World Tour agreed to grant conditional releases with nine players this season, it is understood the change for 2027 is predominantly down to LIV offering players equity in future and a feeling this is incompatible with the European tour being a members organisation.

However, it also comes at a time when the DP World Tour's strategic alliance with the PGA Tour is being negotiated, so the move likely reflects a desire to put itself in the best position possible in those discussions.

Players will have until 16 November to sign up to the DP World Tour for next year.

Under the terms of its court-supervised restructuring process, LIV Golf needs to sign players up by 25 October.

Ted Goldthorpe, head of BC Partners Credit, told BBC Sport last week he was "confident" LIV would have a "critical mass" of players.

But since then two-time major winner Rahm has said he will not continue playing on the LIV tour.

Lawyers representing a number of other players, including fellow major winners Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith, sought clarification from the court that rejection of contracts would equate to "termination", enabling players to hold discussions with third parties about their futures.

Richard Bland is currently the only player to have stated publicly a desire to play on LIV 2.0.

However, Perez indicated last month he hoped there would be a future for the league.

title: Former Ryder Cup captain backs DPWT as LIV Golf players face major decision

title: Jon Rahm reveals first start since LIV Golf exit

“Mr. Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0… and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” said the Spaniard’s attorney, John Beck.

Rahm will tee it up next month in the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship – which will, somewhat peculiarly, be his first start in the DP World Tour Playoffs event.

The two-time major champion has won the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in Dubai on three occasions, but has never played in the Abu Dhabi precursor.

“I’ve had some of the best weeks of my career in the UAE, so I’m really looking forward to playing in Abu Dhabi for the first time,” Rahm said in a press release.

“I’ve heard great things about Yas Links, and I’m looking forward to playing there. It’ll be great to get started in Abu Dhabi before heading to Dubai the following week.”

Rahm agreed a deal with the DP World Tour earlier this season which stipulated he had to play an additional number of events to avoid being punished for breaking conflicting events rules on LIV Golf.

He will therefore play in Abu Dhabi and, providing he advances through, Tour Championship at Jumeirah Estates the following week as he secures his membership for the 2027 season.

Rahm is currently 46th in the Race to Dubai rankings and the top 50 make it to the $10 million finale. He missed the Open de Espana last week as he and his wife Kelley are expecting a fourth child.

Taiwanese men's, women's doubles pairs lose in BWF Arctic Open finals

Taipei, Oct. 12 (CNA) Taiwanese men's and women's doubles pairs each took home silver medals after losing in the finals of the 2026 Arctic Open, a Badminton World Federation (BWF) Super 500 tournament, in Vantaa, Finland, on Sunday (local time).

In the women's doubles finals, world No. 8 pair Hsu Yin-hui (許尹鏸) and Lin Jhih-yun (林芝昀) lost 21-18, 21-19 to China's Chen Fan Shutian (陳樊淑湉) and Luo Xumin (羅徐敏) in two games that remained neck-and-neck throughout.

Speaking to reporters, Hsu and Lin said the Chinese duo's style of play had kept them on the back foot, and they had been unable to break through their opponents' defense in the closing stages of each game.

The pair noted that Sunday's defeat was the third time they had made the finals and lost in a BWF Super 500 tournament since teaming up in 2023, joking that "maybe the fourth time's a charm."

In men's doubles, Taiwan's Lai Po-yu (賴柏佑) and Tsai Fu-cheng (蔡富丞), both 20, also lost a closely contested 21-19, 21-19 final to Malaysia's Aaron Tai (戴偉欽) and Yap Roy King (葉睿慶).
